Question 1

Which one of the following is concerned with the meaning of a sentence in knowledge representation?

  • A. Structure
  • B. Computational aspect
  • C. Semantics
  • D. Syntax

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 1

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources.

Study-guide sections

AI24 · Represent knowledge for inference

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI24 · Represent knowledge for inference

Correct answer: C — Semantics

Semantics assigns meaning to sentences; syntax restricts their legal construction (PDF p. 43). The stem asks about meaning rather than representation layout or computational efficiency.

Evidence in the complete study note

Knowledge representation encodes facts, objects, relations, events and rules so a machine can use them. Syntax defines legal expressions; semantics defines their meaning. A knowledge base stores assertions; an inference system derives consequences. Declarative knowledge says what is true; procedural knowledge specifies how to act.AI24

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Structure concerns arrangement, not the stated meaning rule. See PDF p. 43.

B · incorrect — Computational aspects concern processing rather than the interpretation definition. See PDF p. 43.

C · correct — This is precisely the module definition of assigning meaning. See PDF p. 43.

D · incorrect — Syntax decides legal symbols and sentence construction. See PDF p. 43.

Question 2

Which one of the following agents works by searching and matching the rules defined by percent and stored internal state?

  • A. Model-based reflex agent
  • B. Goal-based agent
  • C. Simple reflex agent
  • D. Utility based agent

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 7

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description.

Study-guide sections

AI06 · Simple and model-based reflex agents

AI07 · Goals, utility and model updates

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI06 · Simple and model-based reflex agents

AI07 · Goals, utility and model updates

Correct answer: A — Model-based reflex agent

Taking “percent” as a typographical error for percept, the stored internal state records percept history and the model specifies world evolution (PDF p. 14). That distinguishes model-based reflex selection from a simple current-percept rule.

Evidence in the complete study note

A simple reflex agent matches condition–action rules against the current percept only: if dirty, clean. It has no persistent world-state memory. This is adequate when the current observation contains everything needed for its rule, but partial observability can make the same percept require different actions.AI06
A model-based reflex agent maintains internal state using the previous state, previous action, current percept, and models of world change and action effects. It then applies rules to that state. Both kinds can use condition–action rules; memory and a world model distinguish them.AI06
A goal-based agent considers future action sequences that reach a desired state. A utility-based agent compares degrees of desirability and trade-offs, choosing maximum expected utility: EU(a)=Σs P(s|a,evidence)U(s). Reaching the destination is a goal; balancing arrival time, safety and cost requires preferences among outcomes.AI07

Choice by choice

A · correct — Combines a model and retained internal state. See PDF p. 14, 14.

B · incorrect — Goal-based selection needs a desired goal, absent here. See PDF p. 14, 14.

C · incorrect — Ignores percept history and therefore cannot account for the stated memory. See PDF p. 14, 14.

D · incorrect — Requires a utility measurement, absent here. See PDF p. 14, 14.

Question 3

Assume the entire state space and transition model are known for every task below, despite any hidden current state. Which problem/environment coupling is incorrect?

  • A. Contingency problem -> partially observable, non-deterministic
  • B. Multiple state problem deterministic, partially observable
  • C. Exploration problem -> partially observable, deterministic
  • D. Single state problem-> fully observable, deterministic

Adapted from

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 28

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources.

Study-guide sections

AI10 · Single-state, multiple-state and contingency problems

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI10 · Single-state, multiple-state and contingency problems

Correct answer: C — Exploration problem -> partially observable, deterministic

A known deterministic model with incomplete observation can be handled by a belief state representing several possible current states. Unknown state spaces or transition models create the need for exploration; partial observability alone does not. Nondeterministic partial observation can require contingency branches, while full observation with known deterministic transitions supports a single-state formulation. The explicit knowledge assumption therefore makes the exploration pairing the incorrect one.

Evidence in the complete study note

With a known deterministic model and full observation, a single current state can be used. Without observation but with known deterministic transitions, a sensorless or multiple-state problem tracks a belief state: a set of possible states.AI10
Nondeterminism or partial observation may require a contingency plan with branches based on later percepts. Exploration or online search is required when the state space or transition model is unknown; observation alone does not identify this category. These classifications can overlap. A pairing based only on “partially observable, deterministic” cannot distinguish a known sensorless problem from an unknown exploration problem.AI10

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — This is a valid coupling: partial observation and nondeterminism can require contingency branches, so it is not the incorrect pairing.

B · incorrect — This is valid under the known-model assumption: incomplete observation can require a belief state, so it is not selected.

C · correct — This is the incorrect coupling: hidden state with a known deterministic model does not by itself require exploration.

D · incorrect — This is valid: full observation and known deterministic transitions support a single current state.

Question 4

Which one of the following is correct first order logic for the statement "There is someone standing at the door and is tall"?

  • A. ∀x (StandingAt (x; door )
  • B. ∀x ( StandingAt (x; door )^ tall(x))
  • C. ∃x ( StandingAt (x; door )^ tall(x))
  • D. ∃x ( StandingAt (x; door ) -> toll(x))

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 33

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations.

Study-guide sections

AI26 · First-order logic and quantifier scope

AI25 · Propositional logic and models

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI26 · First-order logic and quantifier scope

AI25 · Propositional logic and models

Correct answer: C — ∃x ( StandingAt (x; door )^ tall(x))

“There is someone” requires ∃x, and “standing ... and ... tall” requires StandingAt(x,door) ∧ tall(x), so C asserts one witness with both properties (PDF pp. 46, 49). An implication does not assert its antecedent and therefore cannot assert that anyone is at the door.

Evidence in the complete study note

Use ∀x(Human(x)→Mortal(x)) for all humans, and ∃x(Student(x)∧Tall(x)) for at least one tall student. These are useful translation patterns, not rules forbidding other connectives. ∀x∃y Likes(x,y) allows a different y for each x; ∃y∀x Likes(x,y) requires one shared y. Negation swaps quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x¬P(x). Only occurrences within the correct quantifier’s scope are bound.AI26
Propositional atoms represent whole true-or-false claims. ¬P negates; P∧Q requires both; P∨Q requires at least one; P→Q is false only when P is true and Q false; P↔Q requires matching truth values. Thus P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q. De Morgan gives ¬(P∧Q) ≡ ¬P∨¬Q.AI25

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incomplete formula with a universal quantifier and no tall predicate. See PDF p. 49, 46.

B · incorrect — Claims everyone has both properties rather than at least one person. See PDF p. 49, 46.

C · correct — Existentially binds the same x in both conjuncts. See PDF p. 49, 46.

D · incorrect — Uses implication instead of conjunction and also spells the predicate toll. See PDF p. 49, 46.

Question 5

Which statements are incorrect? Interpret rational action as maximizing expected performance given available information; do not assume a successful action always exists. Select all that apply.

  • A. A rational agent know the result of its action, but unrealistic
  • B. Rational agent take action but not 100% sure of success
  • C. Rational agent act to achieve utmost success based on information
  • D. An omniscience agent takes actions for 100% sure of success

Adapted from

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 57

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description.

Study-guide sections

AI04 · Rationality and performance

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI04 · Rationality and performance

Correct answers (select all): A, D — A rational agent know the result of its action, but unrealistic; An omniscience agent takes actions for 100% sure of success

Rationality concerns choosing the action with the best expected performance given the agent’s information. It does not mean knowing actual outcomes in advance, so the first claim incorrectly attributes omniscience to a rational agent. Even omniscience would not ensure success if all available actions fail. The remaining statements correctly allow uncertainty while requiring the best expected choice under the available evidence.

Evidence in the complete study note

A performance measure defines success externally: safety, useful deliveries, elapsed time, or cost. Rationality depends on that measure, prior knowledge, percept history, and available actions. A rational agent selects the action with the best expected performance given its information.AI04
Omniscience would mean knowing actual action outcomes in advance. Rationality does not require omniscience or guaranteed success. Even complete outcome knowledge cannot create a successful action when every available action fails. Information gathering and exploration may therefore be rational actions.AI04

Choice by choice

A · correct — This is false: rationality does not imply knowing actual action outcomes in advance.

B · incorrect — This is true: a rational action need not guarantee success.

C · incorrect — This is true when utmost success means best expected performance given the available information.

D · correct — This is false: complete outcome knowledge cannot guarantee that a successful action exists.

Question 6

________ finds the shortest path to the goal based on cost.

  • A. Depth first search
  • B. Iterative deepening
  • C. Uniform cost search
  • D. Breath first search

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 59

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI15 · Uniform-cost search and Dijkstra

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI15 · Uniform-cost search and Dijkstra

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

Correct answer: C — Uniform cost search

Uniform-cost search explicitly seeks the goal path with lowest cumulative cost and uses a priority queue (PDF p. 21). “Shortest” here means minimum cost, under the usual nonnegative-cost setting; minimum depth alone is not sufficient when edge costs vary.

Evidence in the complete study note

UCS uses a priority queue ordered by actual accumulated path cost g(n). Remove a minimum-g node; accept a goal when removed, not when first generated. Relax each edge: if a cheaper path is found, update its frontier cost and parent.AI15
With finite branching and each step at least ε>0, UCS is complete and optimal. Finite graphs permit nonnegative edges with proper duplicate handling. Dijkstra uses the same minimum-distance principle, often computing all reachable distances; UCS commonly stops at a goal and generates states on demand. Queue initialization is an implementation choice, not a fundamental distinction. Negative edges invalidate the usual finalized-distance argument.AI15
BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.AI13
DLS runs DFS to depth ℓ and reports cutoff separately from failure. It misses goals deeper than ℓ. Iterative deepening runs DLS with limits 0,1,2,…; for finite b it finds the shallowest solution with O(b^d) time and O(bd) frontier space, optimal for equal step costs. Repeated shallow work is small compared with the deepest level.AI16

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Follows depth and is explicitly nonoptimal on p. 19. See PDF p. 21, 21.

B · incorrect — Increases depth limits, not cumulative-cost priority. See PDF p. 21, 21.

C · correct — Directly minimizes cumulative path cost. See PDF p. 21, 21.

D · incorrect — Minimizes steps; equivalent to UCS only when all edge costs are equal. See PDF p. 21, 21.

Question 7

The data structure used in the standard implementation of Depth First Search is ?

  • A. Stack
  • B. Array
  • C. Linked List
  • D. Queue

Source

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 74

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI14 · Depth-first search

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI-S02 · Ordered lookup versus state-space traversal

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI14 · Depth-first search

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI-S02 · Ordered lookup versus state-space traversal

Correct answer: A — Stack

DFS uses a stack (PDF p. 18): the newest pending state is explored first. Arrays or linked lists could implement a stack, but they do not themselves specify the required access order.

Evidence in the complete study note

DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.AI14
BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.AI13
Binary search exploits the order of a sorted sequence: a comparison narrows the remaining candidate interval instead of exploring arbitrary successor states. Array bisection therefore differs from breadth-first or depth-first traversal of a general state-space graph. A storage container such as an array does not by itself specify FIFO or LIFO frontier behavior.AI-S02

Choice by choice

A · correct — Explicitly named implementation structure. See PDF p. 18.

B · incorrect — May store a stack but does not specify LIFO behavior. See PDF p. 18.

C · incorrect — May implement a stack but is not the stated abstract structure. See PDF p. 18.

D · incorrect — FIFO queue is used for BFS on p. 20. See PDF p. 18.

Question 8

Among the following, which kind of algorithm is used in the Game tree to make decisions of Win/Lose?

  • A. Heuristic Search Algorithm
  • B. Min/Max Algorithm
  • C. Depth First Search Algorithm
  • D. Greedy Search Algorithm

Sources

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 80

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · Sene 2016 · Question 28-2

  • Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 205

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources.

Study-guide sections

AI22 · Games and minimax

AI23 · Alpha–beta and game evaluation

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI22 · Games and minimax

AI23 · Alpha–beta and game evaluation

Correct answer: B — Min/Max Algorithm

Minimax recursively backs up utilities, choosing maxima on MAX turns and minima on MIN turns, so it selects moves against an optimal opponent (PDF pp. 33–34). DFS is its traversal mechanism rather than the adversarial decision rule.

Evidence in the complete study note

Minimax assigns terminal utilities, takes minima at MIN nodes and maxima at MAX nodes, then chooses a maximum-valued root action. It gives the best guaranteed outcome against optimal opposition within the modeled tree. For stochastic outcomes add chance nodes weighted by probabilities.AI22
At a depth cutoff use an evaluation function estimating position desirability. Positive favors the designated MAX player, negative MIN; the scale is a convention, with +1/0/−1 often win/draw/loss. Material counts weighted pieces; mobility counts legal options; territory scores controlled regions. These are different features, often combined. Heuristics improve limited computation, not guarantee victory.AI23

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A broad category, not the specified alternating-player rule. See PDF p. 33, 34.

B · correct — Provides the game-tree decision procedure. See PDF p. 33, 34.

C · incorrect — Traverses the tree but alone does not compare opponent utilities. See PDF p. 33, 34.

D · incorrect — Chooses local heuristic promise rather than alternating MAX/MIN decisions. See PDF p. 33, 34.

AI03 · Agents, percepts and action

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI03 · Agents, percepts and action

Correct answer: B — Agent function is performing

The module evaluates behavior and performance through the agent function, a mapping from perception history to action (PDF p. 11). B is grammatically incomplete but identifies that function.

Evidence in the complete study note

A percept is one observation; a percept sequence is the entire observation history. An agent function maps percept sequences to actions: f:P*→A. An agent program implements that mapping on an architecture; agent = architecture + program. Environment means the setting in which it senses and acts, not merely the search space. Autonomy means relying substantially on experience rather than only a designer’s prior instructions.AI03
An agent perceives an environment through sensors and acts through actuators or effectors. Cameras sense; motors move. Software sensors may be incoming messages and software actions may be API requests. Humans are agents but are not artificial agents.AI03

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Input history alone does not specify the selected actions. See PDF p. 11.

B · correct — Names the function that describes action behavior. See PDF p. 11.

C · incorrect — Describe input/output mechanisms, not the complete action mapping. See PDF p. 11.

D · incorrect — Provides context, not the mapping. See PDF p. 11.

AI07 · Goals, utility and model updates

AI06 · Simple and model-based reflex agents

AI08 · Learning-agent components

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI07 · Goals, utility and model updates

AI06 · Simple and model-based reflex agents

AI08 · Learning-agent components

Correct answer: C — Utility based agent

Happy/unhappy is an informal description of desirability. The utility function assigns each state a real number measuring how well actions achieve goals (PDF p. 15). The module does not literally use those emotional terms.

Evidence in the complete study note

A goal-based agent considers future action sequences that reach a desired state. A utility-based agent compares degrees of desirability and trade-offs, choosing maximum expected utility: EU(a)=Σs P(s|a,evidence)U(s). Reaching the destination is a goal; balancing arrival time, safety and cost requires preferences among outcomes.AI07
A simple reflex agent matches condition–action rules against the current percept only: if dirty, clean. It has no persistent world-state memory. This is adequate when the current observation contains everything needed for its rule, but partial observability can make the same percept require different actions.AI06
The performance element selects actions. The learning element changes the agent to improve future performance. The critic evaluates behavior against a performance standard and supplies feedback. The problem generator suggests exploratory actions likely to yield useful experience.AI08

A · incorrect — Selects current-percept rules, not ranked desirability. See PDF p. 15.

Question 12

Here “exploratory learning” means discovering structure in data without target labels, oracle labeling or reward-driven interaction. Which learning regime is meant?

  • A. Supervised learning
  • B. Active learning
  • C. Unsupervised learning
  • D. Reinforcement learning
  • E. None of the Above

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 84

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality.

Study-guide sections

AI32 · Unsupervised, semi-supervised and active learning

AI33 · Reinforcement learning

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI32 · Unsupervised, semi-supervised and active learning

AI33 · Reinforcement learning

Correct answer: C — Unsupervised learning

Unsupervised learning seeks patterns such as clusters or associations without target labels. Active learning asks an oracle to label selected cases, supervised learning fits labeled input-target examples, and reinforcement learning improves behavior from reward-driven interaction. Specifying the feedback makes the intended use of exploratory precise. The term alone would have several usages, but the stated unlabeled structure-discovery task identifies a definite learning regime.

Evidence in the complete study note

Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features. Good clusters have high within-cluster similarity and low between-cluster similarity under an appropriate distance. K-means alternates assignment to nearest centroids and centroid updates.AI32
Semi-supervised learning combines some labels with additional unlabeled data. Active learning chooses informative cases for an oracle to label; it still uses labels. “Exploratory learning” is not an exclusive standard synonym: it can mean unsupervised exploration or active data acquisition, so define the feedback. A task named summarization or time-series analysis is not automatically supervised; its training targets determine that.AI32
An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label. Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward.AI33

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Supervised learning uses labeled targets, excluded by the stem.

B · incorrect — Active learning obtains oracle labels, excluded by the stem.

C · correct — Unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels.

D · incorrect — Reinforcement learning uses reward-driven interaction, excluded here.

E · incorrect — The specified regime is present among the choices.

Question 13

Let F(x,y,t) mean that person x can fool person y at time t. Over nonempty person and time domains, which statement is equivalent to ∀x∃y∃t ¬F(x,y,t)?

  • A. Everyone can fool some person at some time
  • B. Every person has someone whom they cannot fool at any time.
  • C. No person can fool any person at any time.
  • D. No one can fool everyone all the time

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 85

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations.

Study-guide sections

AI26 · First-order logic and quantifier scope

AI44 · Interpret quantified statements and search assumptions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI26 · First-order logic and quantifier scope

AI44 · Interpret quantified statements and search assumptions

Correct answer: D — No one can fool everyone all the time

For each person x, the formula requires a person y and a time t for which fooling fails. Moving negation across the quantifiers gives ¬∃x∀y∀t F(x,y,t): nobody can fool everyone all the time. The witness and time can depend on x. Requiring failure at every time, or forbidding all fooling events, would be stronger claims.

Evidence in the complete study note

Use ∀x(Human(x)→Mortal(x)) for all humans, and ∃x(Student(x)∧Tall(x)) for at least one tall student. These are useful translation patterns, not rules forbidding other connectives. ∀x∃y Likes(x,y) allows a different y for each x; ∃y∀x Likes(x,y) requires one shared y. Negation swaps quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x¬P(x). Only occurrences within the correct quantifier’s scope are bound.AI26
The formula ∀x∃y∃t¬F(x,y,t) means that for each person there is a person and time at which fooling fails. By quantifier negation this is ¬∃x∀y∀t F(x,y,t), so nobody fools everybody all the time. Forbidding every successful instance is a much stronger claim than this formula.AI44

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — This asserts a successful fooling event for each person, rather than an unsuccessful event.

B · incorrect — This requires one witness person who cannot be fooled at every time, a stronger time scope than the formula requires.

C · incorrect — This forbids all fooling events, much stronger than requiring one unsuccessful event for each person.

D · correct — Negating someone fooling everyone at every time yields, for each person, someone and some time when fooling fails.

Question 14

A language system must decide which interpretation is intended when a sentence permits more than one meaning or grammatical attachment. Which NLP challenge does this describe?

  • A. Handling Tokenization
  • B. Handling Ambiguity of Sentences
  • C. Handling POS-Tagging
  • D. Handling Semantics of Sentences
  • E. All of the mentioned

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 86

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Match the input, output and purpose to the appropriate language, perception or physical-action task.

Study-guide sections

AI37 · Language processing tasks

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI37 · Language processing tasks

Correct answer: B — Handling Ambiguity of Sentences

The difficulty described is ambiguity: a word or sentence can permit multiple meanings or structural attachments. Tokenization creates units, POS tagging assigns grammatical roles, and semantic analysis concerns meaning. These tasks can help resolve ambiguity, but they are not synonymous with the particular obstacle. The question therefore asks for the named challenge rather than ranking all NLP difficulties.

Evidence in the complete study note

Tokenization divides text into processing units; tokens may be words, punctuation or subwords. POS tagging assigns grammatical roles; named-entity recognition identifies people, organizations and locations. Parsing identifies grammatical structure; semantics concerns meaning; discourse links sentences; pragmatics uses context and speaker intent. Sentiment analysis predicts evaluative tone. Ambiguity can occur at every level: “bank” has multiple senses, and “I saw the man with a telescope” has multiple attachments.AI37
NLP interprets and generates human language: translation, dialogue, summarization, question answering and text generation. Speech recognition converts audio to text; speech synthesis generates speech. They overlap language processing but solve different input/output tasks.AI37

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Tokenization decides processing units; it does not name the existence of multiple interpretations.

B · correct — Ambiguity means that more than one interpretation is possible.

C · incorrect — POS tagging assigns grammatical categories rather than naming the competing interpretations.

D · incorrect — Semantics studies meaning generally; the specific obstacle described is multiplicity of interpretations.

E · incorrect — This includes tokenization, tagging and semantic analysis in general, which do not all name the specific multiple-interpretation obstacle.

Study-guide sections

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI-S02 · Ordered lookup versus state-space traversal

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI-S02 · Ordered lookup versus state-space traversal

Correct answer: B — Informed search

Informed search uses problem-specific heuristic information to estimate remaining cost or promise. Merely retaining the current state would not establish that category, because uninformed search also uses states, successors and known costs. The revised stem supplies the missing estimate. Binary search concerns an ordered interval rather than this state-space frontier, and circular traversal does not identify the heuristic-informed category being tested.

Evidence in the complete study note

A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost or evaluates promise using problem-specific knowledge. It can reduce explored work, but computing it also costs time. Uninformed algorithms use only the problem definition and known costs; UCS remains uninformed despite using g.AI17
Binary search exploits the order of a sorted sequence: a comparison narrows the remaining candidate interval instead of exploring arbitrary successor states. Array bisection therefore differs from breadth-first or depth-first traversal of a general state-space graph. A storage container such as an array does not by itself specify FIFO or LIFO frontier behavior.AI-S02

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Uninformed search lacks the extra remaining-cost heuristic specified here.

B · correct — Informed search uses problem-specific heuristic estimates to guide the frontier.

C · incorrect — Traversal without heuristic estimates does not meet the specified remaining-cost-guided strategy.

D · incorrect — Binary search needs an ordered search interval, not merely goal-directed state exploration.

An agent’s actions affect later decisions; identical state-action pairs can have different outcomes; and the world changes while the agent deliberates. Which list describes these three properties?

  • A. Deterministic, fully observable, static
  • B. Fully observable, sequential, deterministic
  • C. Partially observable, static, continuous
  • D. Sequential, non-deterministic, dynamic

  • Mock exam 4 · Question 2

  • National Computer Science Exit Exam · Question 64

  • National Computer Science Exit Exam

Alternative version 1

  • A. Partially observable, non-deterministic, sequential, dynamic
  • B. Deterministic, sequential (non-episodic), dynamic, continuous
  • C. Static, episodic, continuous, partially observable
  • D. Fully observable, discrete, episodic, static
Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Read the relevant agent component, action-selection criterion or environment dimension. Use only properties established by the description.

Study-guide sections

AI09 · Environment dimensions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI09 · Environment dimensions

Correct answer: D — Sequential, non-deterministic, dynamic

The scenario establishes three independent dimensions. Earlier actions affect later decisions, so it is sequential. Outcomes are not fixed by the state-action pair, so it is non-deterministic. Change during deliberation makes it dynamic. It gives no complete observation or continuity specification. Classifying the stated properties avoids an unsupported universal ranking of how difficult different environments must be.

Evidence in the complete study note

Fully observable means sensors reveal relevant state; partially observable means relevant information is hidden or noisy. Deterministic means state and action determine the next state; stochastic means outcomes involve randomness. Strategic uncertainty about an opponent is distinct from dice-like randomness.AI09
Episodic decisions are independent; sequential decisions affect later situations. Static worlds do not change while deliberating; dynamic ones do. A clock affecting score makes an otherwise static game semidynamic. Discrete quantities have distinct alternatives; continuous quantities vary along real-valued ranges. Known versus unknown concerns knowledge of the transition model, not observability.AI09

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Determinism and a static world contradict the uncertain outcomes and ongoing change.

B · incorrect — Sequential fits, but deterministic outcomes contradict the scenario.

C · incorrect — A static environment cannot change while the agent deliberates; this list also omits the stated action dependence.

D · correct — Sequential captures dependent decisions, non-deterministic captures uncertain outcomes, and dynamic captures change during deliberation.

Alternative version 1

Correct answer: A — Partially observable, non-deterministic, sequential, dynamic

Incomplete observations establish partial observability, uncertain transitions establish non-determinism, consequences for later decisions establish sequentiality, and change during deliberation establishes dynamics. The other lists contradict at least one of those conditions. No universal difficulty comparison is needed.

Fully observable means sensors reveal relevant state; partially observable means relevant information is hidden or noisy. Deterministic means state and action determine the next state; stochastic means outcomes involve randomness. Strategic uncertainty about an opponent is distinct from dice-like randomness.AI09

Episodic decisions are independent; sequential decisions affect later situations. Static worlds do not change while deliberating; dynamic ones do. A clock affecting score makes an otherwise static game semidynamic. Discrete quantities have distinct alternatives; continuous quantities vary along real-valued ranges. Known versus unknown concerns knowledge of the transition model, not observability.AI09

A · correct — All four properties match the stated scenario.

B · incorrect — Determinism contradicts uncertain transition outcomes.

C · incorrect — Static and episodic contradict ongoing change and consequences for later decisions.

D · incorrect — Full observability, episodicity and static conditions each contradict the scenario.

The wording reproduces the two model-based factors: knowledge of how the world changes and a current-state representation based on percept history (PDF p. 14). No explicit goal or utility comparison is requested.

Evidence in the complete study note

A model-based reflex agent maintains internal state using the previous state, previous action, current percept, and models of world change and action effects. It then applies rules to that state. Both kinds can use condition–action rules; memory and a world model distinguish them.AI06

Question 18

An evaluation technique of classifier accuracy where we randomly partition the data into k mutually exclusive subsets, each approximately equal size and, use Di as test set and others as training set at i-th iteration is ______.

  • A. Random sampling
  • B. Cross-validation
  • C. Stratified cross-validation
  • D. Holdout method

Source

  • Mock exam 4 · Question 4

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Identify the training feedback, prediction target or measured error. Keep learning objectives separate from model architecture and data modality.

Study-guide sections

AI35 · Generalization and validation

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI35 · Generalization and validation

Correct answer: B — k-fold cross-validation.

AI35 describes exactly the rotation in the stem: build k models, each trained on all folds except one, evaluate on that held-out fold, then average the scores. The stem does not say class proportions are preserved, so stratification is not established. A single holdout split or generic random sampling does not specify this complete rotation.

Evidence in the complete study note

Train data fits parameters; validation data selects models or settings; a held-out test set estimates final performance. In k-fold validation, train k models, each on k−1 folds and evaluate on the remaining fold, then average scores. Stratification approximately preserves label proportions. Fit preprocessing within each training fold. Time-ordered data needs splits respecting time; repeated tuning on the final test set leaks information.AI35

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Random sampling alone does not specify the disjoint k-fold rotation of training and test subsets.

B · correct — The described repeated use of each fold as the held-out subset is k-fold cross-validation.

C · incorrect — Stratification additionally preserves label proportions, a condition not supplied by equal fold sizes alone.

D · incorrect — A holdout method uses a fixed split rather than rotating through all k disjoint test folds.

AI31 · Supervised learning and prediction

AI32 · Unsupervised, semi-supervised and active learning

AI33 · Reinforcement learning

Correct answer: C — Classification

First, second and third generation are supplied category names. Treating the task as assigning institutions to these predefined labels makes it classification, which the module lists under supervised learning (PDF p. 69). If categories were to be discovered without labels, clustering would instead be relevant.

Evidence in the complete study note

Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples. Classification predicts discrete labels, such as institution generations or spam/nonspam; regression predicts numeric quantities, such as prices. Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast outcomes and can use either. Specify the target before choosing a method.AI31
Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features. Good clusters have high within-cluster similarity and low between-cluster similarity under an appropriate distance. K-means alternates assignment to nearest centroids and centroid updates.AI32
An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label. Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward.AI33

C · correct — Matches assignment to the supplied categories. See PDF p. 69, 69.

D · incorrect — Discovers groupings from inputs rather than assigning known labels. See PDF p. 69, 69.

Question 23

What is completeness of search algorithms?

  • A. If there is a difference between the quality of goal states, the agent will find the best one
  • B. An estimate of how much information the algorithm needs to store for finding a solution
  • C. An estimate of how many search steps it takes to find a solution
  • D. Provided that a solution exists, the algorithm will find it

Sources

  • Computer Science model exam · Question 57

  • University of Gondar model exam · Question 57

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI12 · Frontiers and evaluation criteria

AI13 · Breadth-first search

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI12 · Frontiers and evaluation criteria

AI13 · Breadth-first search

Correct answer: D — Provided that a solution exists, the algorithm will find it

Completeness is the guarantee of finding a solution when an appropriately reachable solution exists; the BFS paragraph illustrates it using a finite-depth goal (PDF p. 20). It is distinct from finding the lowest-cost solution and from time or memory requirements.

Evidence in the complete study note

Completeness means finding a solution if one exists under stated assumptions; optimality means returning the best solution. Time counts work, often generated nodes; space counts simultaneous storage. Let b be branching factor, d shallowest goal depth, m maximum search depth, and ℓ a depth limit. Graph-search bounds in vertices V and edges E differ from implicit-tree bounds.AI12
BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.AI13

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Defines optimality, not completeness. See PDF p. 20, 18.

B · incorrect — Describes space complexity. See PDF p. 20, 18.

C · incorrect — Describes time complexity. See PDF p. 20, 18.

D · correct — Matches solution-finding guarantee. See PDF p. 20, 18.

Study-guide sections

AI03 · Agents, percepts and action

AI04 · Rationality and performance

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI03 · Agents, percepts and action

AI04 · Rationality and performance

Correct answer: A — An artificial agent that selects actions for the best expected performance given its percept history and knowledge.

A rational artificial agent senses its environment and chooses actions expected to maximize its performance measure given its information. It need not know actual outcomes in advance. Sensors and effectors alone do not supply an action-selection policy, and combining two vaguely named agent categories is not the architecture-plus-program definition. The choice gives the intended rational-agent criterion without imposing omniscience.

Evidence in the complete study note

An agent perceives an environment through sensors and acts through actuators or effectors. Cameras sense; motors move. Software sensors may be incoming messages and software actions may be API requests. Humans are agents but are not artificial agents.AI03
A percept is one observation; a percept sequence is the entire observation history. An agent function maps percept sequences to actions: f:P*→A. An agent program implements that mapping on an architecture; agent = architecture + program. Environment means the setting in which it senses and acts, not merely the search space. Autonomy means relying substantially on experience rather than only a designer’s prior instructions.AI03
A performance measure defines success externally: safety, useful deliveries, elapsed time, or cost. Rationality depends on that measure, prior knowledge, percept history, and available actions. A rational agent selects the action with the best expected performance given its information.AI04

Choice by choice

A · correct — This states the rational action-selection criterion without requiring omniscience.

B · incorrect — Sensors and effectors provide interaction, but alone do not establish intelligent action selection.

C · incorrect — Architecture plus program is not a combination of a software agent and a hardware agent.

D · incorrect — The component statements are defective, so their aggregate is not a valid definition.

Which types of searching strategies is not grouped under blind search?

  • A. Breadth first search
  • B. Uniform cost search
  • C. Constraint satisfaction search
  • D. Depth limited search

Source

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 120

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI21 · Constraint satisfaction

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI21 · Constraint satisfaction

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

Correct answer: C — Constraint satisfaction search

BFS, UCS and depth-limited search appear in the uninformed-search sequence (PDF pp. 18–22). Constraint satisfaction is treated separately, so C is the item not grouped under blind search.

Evidence in the complete study note

Backtracking assigns a variable, tries a legal value, and undoes the choice on failure. Choose the variable with fewest remaining values; break ties by degree; try values that rule out fewest neighbor choices. Forward checking removes incompatible neighbor values. Arc consistency removes a value when a binary constraint offers it no support in the other domain. CSP is a problem framework using search and propagation, not a universal fourth uninformed traversal.AI21
A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost or evaluates promise using problem-specific knowledge. It can reduce explored work, but computing it also costs time. Uninformed algorithms use only the problem definition and known costs; UCS remains uninformed despite using g.AI17
BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.AI13
DLS runs DFS to depth ℓ and reports cutoff separately from failure. It misses goals deeper than ℓ. Iterative deepening runs DLS with limits 0,1,2,…; for finite b it finds the shallowest solution with O(b^d) time and O(bd) frontier space, optimal for equal step costs. Repeated shallow work is small compared with the deepest level.AI16

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — BFS is in the uninformed sequence. See PDF p. 18, 21, 36.

B · incorrect — UCS is in the uninformed sequence. See PDF p. 18, 21, 36.

C · correct — A separately presented constraint-based problem formulation/search topic. See PDF p. 18, 21, 36.

D · incorrect — Depth-limited search is in the uninformed sequence. See PDF p. 18, 21, 36.

Question 39

Which statement correctly distinguishes propositional logic from first-order logic?

  • A. It evaluates whole propositions using a truth assignment, without quantifying over objects in a domain.
  • B. It is predicate logic
  • C. It assigns truth to open predicates without assigning values to their object variables.
  • D. It contains quantifier

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 124

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations.

Study-guide sections

AI26 · First-order logic and quantifier scope

AI25 · Propositional logic and models

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI26 · First-order logic and quantifier scope

AI25 · Propositional logic and models

Correct answer: A — It evaluates whole propositions using a truth assignment, without quantifying over objects in a domain.

Propositional logic treats atoms as whole true-or-false claims and evaluates compound formulas from a truth assignment. It does not quantify over individual objects. First-order logic adds predicates, object variables, interpretations and quantifiers. The distinction does not mean that propositional truth needs no assignment: the truth values of its atoms still matter.

Evidence in the complete study note

First-order logic adds objects, predicates, functions and quantified object variables. Human(a) is a property; Likes(a,b) a relation; father(a) a function term. Propositional logic has no object quantifiers, but its truth still depends on the assigned atom values.AI26
Propositional atoms represent whole true-or-false claims. ¬P negates; P∧Q requires both; P∨Q requires at least one; P→Q is false only when P is true and Q false; P↔Q requires matching truth values. Thus P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q. De Morgan gives ¬(P∧Q) ≡ ¬P∨¬Q.AI25

Choice by choice

A · correct — Propositional evaluation uses atom truth values rather than object-domain quantification.

B · incorrect — Propositional logic is not identical to first-order predicate logic.

C · incorrect — Open predicates need interpretation and variable assignments; this is not a propositional truth rule.

D · incorrect — Object quantifiers belong to first-order logic, not propositional syntax.

Question 41

algorithm traverses a graph in a Breadth-ward motion and uses a queue to remember to get the next vertex to start a search, when a dead end occurs in any iteration.

  • A. Breadth first search
  • B. Binary search
  • C. Depth first search
  • D. A&C

Source

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Study-guide sections

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI14 · Depth-first search

AI-S02 · Ordered lookup versus state-space traversal

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI14 · Depth-first search

AI-S02 · Ordered lookup versus state-space traversal

Correct answer: A — Breadth first search

Expanding a graph breadthwise with a FIFO queue is precisely BFS (PDF pp. 19–20). DFS follows a path deeply and uses a stack; binary search is not this traversal.

Evidence in the complete study note

BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.AI13
DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.AI14
Binary search exploits the order of a sorted sequence: a comparison narrows the remaining candidate interval instead of exploring arbitrary successor states. Array bisection therefore differs from breadth-first or depth-first traversal of a general state-space graph. A storage container such as an array does not by itself specify FIFO or LIFO frontier behavior.AI-S02

Choice by choice

A · correct — Matches breadthwise expansion and FIFO frontier. See PDF p. 19, 20.

B · incorrect — Not the stated graph traversal. See PDF p. 19, 20.

C · incorrect — DFS uses a stack and goes deeply first. See PDF p. 19, 20.

D · incorrect — DFS does not meet the queue/breadthwise description. See PDF p. 19, 20.

Question 43

Why is Greedy Best-First Search not guaranteed to be optimal or complete?

  • A. It ignores path cost g( n) and relies only on h(n)
  • B. It always chooses the shallowest node
  • C. . It expands nodes in FIFO order
  • D. It requires full knowledge of the goal state in advance

Source

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 8

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

Correct answer: A — It ignores path cost g( n) and relies only on h(n)

Greedy chooses by estimated remaining cost h(n), ignoring accumulated path cost g(n), so a promising estimate can hide an expensive route. The module also warns of loops and nonoptimality (PDF pp. 25–26). Completeness depends on implementation and state-space assumptions; the general guarantee is absent.

Evidence in the complete study note

Best-first is a family that orders OPEN by an evaluation function. Greedy best-first uses f=h and removes the smallest estimate, ignoring the cost already paid. It can choose an expensive route, loop without duplicate checks, or follow an infinite misleading branch. On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, but not generally optimal. Its implicit finite-tree worst case can be O(b^m).AI17
A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.AI18

Choice by choice

A · correct — Its h-only choice gives the stated lack of a general guarantee. See PDF p. 25, 26.

B · incorrect — Shallowest-first describes BFS. See PDF p. 25, 26.

C · incorrect — FIFO order describes BFS, not heuristic priority. See PDF p. 25, 26.

D · incorrect — Not the reason the module gives for greedy failures. See PDF p. 25, 26.

Best-first is a family that orders OPEN by an evaluation function. Greedy best-first uses f=h and removes the smallest estimate, ignoring the cost already paid. It can choose an expensive route, loop without duplicate checks, or follow an infinite misleading branch. On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, but not generally optimal. Its implicit finite-tree worst case can be O(b^m).AI17

Choice by choice

A · correct — Direct definition. See PDF p. 25.

B · incorrect — An estimate does not itself specify a guaranteed optimal path. See PDF p. 25.

C · incorrect — Repeated-state management is a separate search concern. See PDF p. 25.

D · incorrect — Brute force is the uninformed contrast. See PDF p. 25.

Question 46

Which type of heuristic search strategy that evaluates nodes by combining g (n), the cost to reach the node, and h ( n.), the cost to get from the node to the goal: f (n) = g (n) +h ( n) Since g( n) gives the path cost from the start node to node n, and h(n) is the estimated cost of the cheapest path from n to the goal, we have f ( n) = estimated cost of the cheapest solution through n ?

  • A. A* search
  • B. Greedy Best-First Search
  • C. Uniform-cost search
  • D. Depth-first search

Adapted from

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 52

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI15 · Uniform-cost search and Dijkstra

AI14 · Depth-first search

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI15 · Uniform-cost search and Dijkstra

AI14 · Depth-first search

Correct answer: A — A* search

A* uses f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining the cost already paid with an estimate of the remaining cost. Greedy best-first uses only h; uniform-cost search uses only g; depth-first search follows its stack discipline. The sum is the distinguishing rule. The stray answer annotation attached to the depth-first option has been removed from the practice choices.

Evidence in the complete study note

A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.AI18
Best-first is a family that orders OPEN by an evaluation function. Greedy best-first uses f=h and removes the smallest estimate, ignoring the cost already paid. It can choose an expensive route, loop without duplicate checks, or follow an infinite misleading branch. On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, but not generally optimal. Its implicit finite-tree worst case can be O(b^m).AI17
UCS uses a priority queue ordered by actual accumulated path cost g(n). Remove a minimum-g node; accept a goal when removed, not when first generated. Relax each edge: if a cheaper path is found, update its frontier cost and parent.AI15
DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.AI14

Choice by choice

A · correct — A* ranks by accumulated path cost plus estimated remaining cost.

B · incorrect — Greedy best-first ranks by h alone and omits accumulated cost.

C · incorrect — Uniform-cost search ranks by g alone and omits the heuristic estimate.

D · incorrect — DFS follows a stack order rather than minimum g+h.

Why is perception still a challenge for AI—even though systems can recognize faces?

  • B. Because AI lacks actuators
  • C. Because open-world inputs may contain occlusion, noise, unfamiliar conditions and incomplete context.

Study-guide references

AI39 · Perception, vision and robotics

AI01 · AI capabilities and scope

Correct answer: C — Because open-world inputs may contain occlusion, noise, unfamiliar conditions and incomplete context.

Recognizing faces in some settings does not solve all perception problems. Occlusion can hide relevant features, noise can corrupt observations, and unfamiliar conditions or missing context can make an interpretation unreliable. These are difficulties in interpreting sensory information. They do not require every perception task to use natural-language understanding, and they are distinct from actuator availability or sensor price.

Evidence in the complete study note

Computer vision interprets images or video: classification names image content, detection locates objects, segmentation labels pixels, and recognition identifies objects or people. Occlusion, lighting change, noise, unfamiliar conditions and incomplete context make open-world perception difficult even when a face detector works well.AI39
Narrow or weak AI addresses bounded tasks, such as face recognition, spam filtering or a voice assistant. General AI denotes broad competence transferable across domains; strong AI also has a philosophical meaning involving actual understanding. Do not equate a humanoid body, autonomous vehicle, or many features with general intelligence.AI01

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Perception can use context and support reasoning; it is not unrelated to it.

B · incorrect — Actuators implement actions, while the question concerns difficulty interpreting sensory input.

C · correct — Occlusion, noise and unfamiliar or incomplete context can defeat otherwise successful recognition systems.

D · incorrect — Cost is not the conceptual reason that open-world interpretation remains difficult.

Question 48

  • B. Reinforcement learning

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI33 · Reinforcement learning

AI32 · Unsupervised, semi-supervised and active learning

AI31 · Supervised learning and prediction

Correct answer: B — Reinforcement learning

Reinforcement learning gives rewards for right actions and penalties for wrong ones, with the goal of obtaining the most reward points (PDF p. 69). B matches both interaction and feedback.

Evidence in the complete study note

An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label. Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward.AI33
Semi-supervised learning combines some labels with additional unlabeled data. Active learning chooses informative cases for an oracle to label; it still uses labels. “Exploratory learning” is not an exclusive standard synonym: it can mean unsupervised exploration or active data acquisition, so define the feedback. A task named summarization or time-series analysis is not automatically supervised; its training targets determine that.AI32
Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples. Classification predicts discrete labels, such as institution generations or spam/nonspam; regression predicts numeric quantities, such as prices. Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast outcomes and can use either. Specify the target before choosing a method.AI31

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Supervised learning uses input–target labels rather than action-reward feedback.

B · correct — Reinforcement learning improves decisions to maximize cumulative reward from interaction.

C · incorrect — Semi-supervised learning mixes labeled and unlabeled examples; that mixture does not define cumulative-reward learning.

D · incorrect — Unsupervised learning discovers unlabeled structure rather than defining an action-reward objective.

Question 49

Which one of the following is wrongly matched as AI environment property pairs?

  • A. Fully observable <-> Partially observable
  • B. Discrete <-> Continuous
  • C. Deterministic <-> Stochastic
  • D. Static <-> Stochastic

Sources

  • National Exit Exam practice questions · Question 9

Study-guide sections

AI09 · Environment dimensions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI09 · Environment dimensions

Correct answer: D — Static <-> Stochastic

The module pairs static with dynamic, and deterministic with nondeterministic (PDF p. 13). Thus static versus stochastic mixes two independent dimensions; D is the wrong pairing.

Evidence in the complete study note

Fully observable means sensors reveal relevant state; partially observable means relevant information is hidden or noisy. Deterministic means state and action determine the next state; stochastic means outcomes involve randomness. Strategic uncertainty about an opponent is distinct from dice-like randomness.AI09
Episodic decisions are independent; sequential decisions affect later situations. Static worlds do not change while deliberating; dynamic ones do. A clock affecting score makes an otherwise static game semidynamic. Discrete quantities have distinct alternatives; continuous quantities vary along real-valued ranges. Known versus unknown concerns knowledge of the transition model, not observability.AI09

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Opposite observability properties. See PDF p. 13, 13.

B · incorrect — Opposite state/action granularity properties. See PDF p. 13, 13.

C · incorrect — Stochastic is the question’s term for nondeterministic transition uncertainty. See PDF p. 13, 13.

D · correct — Incorrect pair: static’s counterpart is dynamic. See PDF p. 13, 13.

Which option describes general data processing without AI learning or inference, rather than naming an AI-related field?

  • A. Machine learning

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI01 · AI capabilities and scope

AI39 · Perception, vision and robotics

AI37 · Language processing tasks

Correct answer: C — Data analysis limited to fixed arithmetic summaries, without learning or inference.

Machine learning develops systems that improve from experience, natural language processing interprets or generates language, and robotics combines sensing, planning and physical action. Data analysis is broader: it may use AI, but fixed arithmetic summaries alone need not involve learning or inference. The option restricts that broad category to ordinary non-AI processing, avoiding the incorrect claim that all data analysis lies outside AI.

Evidence in the complete study note

Artificial intelligence studies systems that perform tasks requiring intelligence: reasoning, learning, planning, perception and language. Applied AI builds useful solutions; cognitive AI uses computational models to investigate biological intelligence. A model should be compared with human behavior or experimental observations before claiming it explains human thought.AI01
Robotics combines mechanical, electrical, control and computing systems to sense, plan and act physically. Components include sensors, controller, power supply, actuators and an end effector. Locomotion may be legged, wheeled or tracked, with trade-offs in terrain, stability and efficiency. Software can act autonomously without being a robot. Humanoid shape is not evidence of general intelligence.AI39
NLP interprets and generates human language: translation, dialogue, summarization, question answering and text generation. Speech recognition converts audio to text; speech synthesis generates speech. They overlap language processing but solve different input/output tasks.AI37

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Machine learning is part of AI, and AI43 explicitly places learning architectures and regimes within it.

B · incorrect — Robotics combines sensing, planning and physical action and is treated as an AI-related field in AI39.

C · correct — The restricted fixed-summary task need not use AI; this does not exclude learning-based data analysis.

D · incorrect — Natural language processing interprets and generates human language and is covered as an AI field in AI37.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI43 · Clarify overlapping learning and AI labels

AI40 · Expert systems and choosing methods

Correct answers (select all): A, B, C — Artificial neural networks; Genetic algorithms; Reinforcement learning

Neural-network training adjusts weights from experience, genetic algorithms evolve candidates using fitness and variation, and reinforcement learning improves policies using rewards from interaction. These are different improvement mechanisms that satisfy the broader capability requested. A fixed expert system applies encoded domain knowledge and does not inherently revise itself through experience. The fixed-system assumption distinguishes using knowledge from learning or optimizing with feedback.

Evidence in the complete study note

ANNs, genetic search and reinforcement learning all improve candidate behavior or performance through experience in different ways. Deep learning is an architecture family usable with supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement objectives. Decision trees and deep models may both be supervised. To distinguish learning regimes, specify labels, reward or unlabeled structure.AI43
An expert system applies specialized knowledge to a domain such as equipment diagnosis. The domain expert supplies expertise; the knowledge engineer elicits and encodes it; the inference engine reasons over a knowledge base and working facts. The user interface handles interaction; an explanation facility presents why or how a conclusion was reached.AI40

Choice by choice

B · correct — Genetic search improves a candidate population through fitness-based experience and variation.

C · correct — RL improves policies from action outcomes and rewards.

D · incorrect — A conventional fixed expert system applies encoded knowledge without inherently learning from experience.

Correct answer: C — To simulate human intelligence

Humanlike AI approaches aim to model human thought or produce humanlike behavior. Simulating aspects of human intelligence expresses that goal. Autonomous action, automation and efficiency can also be useful AI objectives, but none requires human imitation. Replacing workers is a social or deployment choice rather than the field’s defining aim. This classification does not impose one primary goal on every AI system.

Evidence in the complete study note

Artificial intelligence studies systems that perform tasks requiring intelligence: reasoning, learning, planning, perception and language. Applied AI builds useful solutions; cognitive AI uses computational models to investigate biological intelligence. A model should be compared with human behavior or experimental observations before claiming it explains human thought.AI01
Thinking humanly models human mental processes; thinking rationally derives conclusions by valid logic. Acting humanly seeks humanlike behavior; acting rationally selects actions expected to achieve objectives. Thought processes and observed behavior are different evaluation targets.AI02
Face recognition is both an applied task and a narrow capability. Broad machine-intelligence goals can include emulating human intelligence and building systems that learn. Humanlike problem-solving alone does not uniquely select expert systems. Python is widely used, but C++ and Java also implement AI; “commonly used” does not isolate one language. McCarthy is associated with naming AI, not its sole invention.AI43

C · correct — Simulating human intelligence expresses the humanlike approach to thought or behavior.

D · incorrect — Automation and efficiency can be achieved without modeling human intelligence.

Question 58

Which AI technique aims to mimic the structure and function of the human brain?

  • A. Genetic algorithms
  • B. Neural networks
  • C. Expert systems
  • D. Reinforcement learning

Source

  • Artificial Intelligence practice questions · Question 9

AI20 · Local optimization and evolutionary search

AI40 · Expert systems and choosing methods

AI33 · Reinforcement learning

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI34 · Neural networks and deep learning

AI20 · Local optimization and evolutionary search

AI40 · Expert systems and choosing methods

AI33 · Reinforcement learning

Correct answer: B — Neural networks

Artificial neural networks are brain-inspired abstractions built from connected processing units with adjustable weights. This is inspiration rather than a literal recreation of the brain. Genetic algorithms use evolutionary population mechanisms, expert systems use encoded domain knowledge, and reinforcement learning defines a feedback regime that can be implemented with many model types, including neural networks.

Evidence in the complete study note

A neuron computes z=Σiwixi+b and output a=φ(z). For x=(2,1), w=(0.5,−1), b=0.2, z=0.2. Linear activation returns z; sigmoid returns 1/(1+e^(−z)); tanh is bipolar; ReLU returns max(0,z). Nonlinearities let multiple layers represent nonlinear relationships.AI34
A genetic algorithm maintains a population, evaluates fitness, selects parents, applies crossover and mutation, and repeats replacement. It searches without guaranteeing global optimality. Means–ends analysis selects a difference between current and goal states, chooses an operator reducing it, and recursively solves its preconditions. Neither method is simply A* running backward.AI20
An expert system applies specialized knowledge to a domain such as equipment diagnosis. The domain expert supplies expertise; the knowledge engineer elicits and encodes it; the inference engine reasons over a knowledge base and working facts. The user interface handles interaction; an explanation facility presents why or how a conclusion was reached.AI40
An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label. Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward.AI33
Feedforward networks pass signals toward outputs without recurrent state loops; recurrent networks carry state across sequence steps. Training adjusts weights, often through gradients and backpropagation. Backpropagation is not the same as a recurrent connection. Deep learning uses multiple representation layers and can learn features from images, sound and text. CNNs share filters across image locations. ANN is a brain-inspired abstraction, not a literal brain simulation; DL⊂ML⊂AI.AI34

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Genetic algorithms are inspired by population selection and genetic variation, not a network of neural processing units.

B · correct — Artificial neural networks are brain-inspired abstractions of interconnected weighted processing units.

C · incorrect — Expert systems encode domain knowledge for inference rather than defining a brain-inspired network structure.

D · incorrect — Reinforcement learning defines reward-based interaction and can use neural or non-neural implementations.

A genetic algorithm maintains a population, evaluates fitness, selects parents, applies crossover and mutation, and repeats replacement. It searches without guaranteeing global optimality. Means–ends analysis selects a difference between current and goal states, chooses an operator reducing it, and recursively solves its preconditions. Neither method is simply A* running backward.AI20

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Data mining is a broader discovery activity; the note names historical-outcome forecasting specifically as predictive analytics.

B · incorrect — Recognizing patterns can support prediction, but does not name the defined historical-forecasting application as precisely.

C · correct — Predictive analytics is explicitly defined as forecasting outcomes using historical patterns.

D · incorrect — Genetic algorithms evolve candidate solutions through fitness and variation, rather than naming historical forecasting itself.

Correct answers (select all): A, B — Autonomous vehicles limited to driving tasks.; Virtual assistants like Siri or Alexa performing bounded assistant tasks.

Narrow AI addresses bounded tasks rather than broad competence transferable across domains. Driving-only automation and a bounded voice assistant therefore establish task-specific capabilities. A humanoid body reveals shape, not intellectual scope, while an unexplained general-purpose label supplies no demonstrated cross-domain competence. The question asks which descriptions establish narrowness, so the two insufficient descriptions are excluded without claiming that their particular robots could never be narrow.

Evidence in the complete study note

Narrow or weak AI addresses bounded tasks, such as face recognition, spam filtering or a voice assistant. General AI denotes broad competence transferable across domains; strong AI also has a philosophical meaning involving actual understanding. Do not equate a humanoid body, autonomous vehicle, or many features with general intelligence.AI01
Robotics combines mechanical, electrical, control and computing systems to sense, plan and act physically. Components include sensors, controller, power supply, actuators and an end effector. Locomotion may be legged, wheeled or tracked, with trade-offs in terrain, stability and efficiency. Software can act autonomously without being a robot. Humanoid shape is not evidence of general intelligence.AI39

Correct answer: A — Reinforcement learning

Reinforcement learning is defined by interaction: the agent acts, receives reward feedback and improves its policy to increase expected cumulative return. Correct-action target labels are not required. Supervised and unsupervised learning use different feedback definitions. Deep learning describes a model architecture and may support reinforcement learning, but it does not name the particular feedback regime asked for.

Evidence in the complete study note

An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label. Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward.AI33
ANNs, genetic search and reinforcement learning all improve candidate behavior or performance through experience in different ways. Deep learning is an architecture family usable with supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement objectives. Decision trees and deep models may both be supervised. To distinguish learning regimes, specify labels, reward or unlabeled structure.AI43
Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples.AI31
Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features.AI32

B · incorrect — Supervised learning uses supplied input–target pairs rather than this reward-feedback definition.

D · incorrect — Deep learning specifies multilayer neural representations and can implement several feedback regimes.
