Study-guide references

AI31 · Supervised learning and prediction

AI43 · Clarify overlapping learning and AI labels

AI34 · Neural networks and deep learning

Correct answer: D — Decision tree learning

A decision tree predicts by testing an attribute at each internal node, following a branch and returning the leaf prediction. Labeled training makes this a supervised classification task. Deep learning can also be supervised, so supervision alone would not distinguish it. The representation in the stem provides the distinction; reinforcement and unsupervised learning describe different feedback regimes.

Evidence in the complete study note

Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples. Classification predicts discrete labels, such as institution generations or spam/nonspam; regression predicts numeric quantities, such as prices. Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast outcomes and can use either. Specify the target before choosing a method.AI31
A decision tree tests an attribute at each internal node, follows the corresponding branch and predicts at a leaf. ID3 chooses high information gain: H(S)=−Σpᵢlog₂pᵢ; gain is parent entropy minus weighted child entropy. Gini impurity is 1−Σpᵢ², zero for a pure class. Pruning limits overfitting. Neural networks, support-vector machines and trees can all be supervised.AI31
ANNs, genetic search and reinforcement learning all improve candidate behavior or performance through experience in different ways. Deep learning is an architecture family usable with supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement objectives. Decision trees and deep models may both be supervised. To distinguish learning regimes, specify labels, reward or unlabeled structure.AI43
Feedforward networks pass signals toward outputs without recurrent state loops; recurrent networks carry state across sequence steps. Training adjusts weights, often through gradients and backpropagation. Backpropagation is not the same as a recurrent connection. Deep learning uses multiple representation layers and can learn features from images, sound and text. CNNs share filters across image locations. ANN is a brain-inspired abstraction, not a literal brain simulation; DL⊂ML⊂AI.AI34

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Reinforcement learning specifies environmental reward feedback rather than this attribute-test representation.

B · incorrect — Unsupervised learning seeks structure without supplied target labels.

C · incorrect — Deep learning uses multiple neural representation layers; it can be supervised but is not the attribute-test-and-leaf model described.

D · correct — Decision tree learning produces attribute-test branches with predictions at leaves.

Study-guide references

AI29 · Probability and uncertain models

AI31 · Supervised learning and prediction

AI33 · Reinforcement learning

AI-S06 · Prediction, transfer and explicit representations

Correct answer: B — Markov models

The Markov assumption makes the current state sufficient for the next-state distribution, rather than requiring the full preceding history. That identifies the model family. Decision trees and support-vector machines are prediction methods with other defining structures. Reinforcement learning is a reward-based learning framework that can use a Markov model, but it is not itself the particular conditional-dependence assumption.

Evidence in the complete study note

A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with conditional probability tables; its joint distribution factors as the product of each node’s probability given its parents. A Markov model assumes the next state depends on the current state rather than the entire past. These represent uncertainty; fuzzy membership represents a different issue.AI29
A decision tree tests an attribute at each internal node, follows the corresponding branch and predicts at a leaf. ID3 chooses high information gain: H(S)=−Σpᵢlog₂pᵢ; gain is parent entropy minus weighted child entropy. Gini impurity is 1−Σpᵢ², zero for a pure class. Pruning limits overfitting. Neural networks, support-vector machines and trees can all be supervised.AI31
An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label. Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward.AI33
Support-vector machines include supervised classification and regression methods. They use support vectors in their decision function rather than being defined by a next-state conditional-dependence assumption. In estimation, variance measures how predictions change across different training samples; overfitting instead names poor generalization caused by fitting training-specific details.AI-S06

Choice by choice

D · incorrect — Reinforcement learning specifies improvement from rewards and may use different model families.

Correct answer: A — Reinforcement learning

Reinforcement learning improves an action policy through rewards received during interaction, with expected cumulative return as the objective. Evidence in the complete study note

An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. ANNs, genetic search and reinforcement learning all improve candidate behavior or performance through experience in different ways. A genetic algorithm maintains a population, evaluates fitness, selects parents, applies crossover and mutation, and repeats replacement. It searches without guaranteeing global optimality. Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features.AI32

Correct answer: B — Machine learning

Evidence in the complete study note

Learning is improvement on task T, measured by P, through experience E. For spam filtering, T is classifying email, E is past labeled messages, and P might be recall at a required precision. Exploration trades immediate reward for information; exploitation uses the best action currently known. Learning can improve reflex, goal-based or utility-based agents.AI08
Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples. Classification predicts discrete labels, such as institution generations or spam/nonspam; regression predicts numeric quantities, such as prices. Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast outcomes and can use either. Specify the target before choosing a method.AI31
Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features. Good clusters have high within-cluster similarity and low between-cluster similarity under an appropriate distance. K-means alternates assignment to nearest centroids and centroid updates.AI32
An expert system applies specialized knowledge to a domain such as equipment diagnosis. The domain expert supplies expertise; the knowledge engineer elicits and encodes it; the inference engine reasons over a knowledge base and working facts. The user interface handles interaction; an explanation facility presents why or how a conclusion was reached.AI40

Question 157

What is the specifically computational-modeling contribution of cognitive AI to studying human thought, as distinct from collecting measurements or running psychological experiments alone?

  • D. By improving computer hardware capabilities

Study-guide sections

AI01 · AI capabilities and scope

AI02 · Four approaches and the Turing test

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI01 · AI capabilities and scope

AI02 · Four approaches and the Turing test

Correct answer: B — By replicating human thought processes

Cognitive AI contributes computational models that implement proposed mechanisms of human thought. Their predictions can then be compared with behavior, response times, errors or other observations. Brain measurements and psychological experiments can provide valuable evidence, but collecting evidence alone is distinct from constructing the computational model. Faster hardware similarly enables work without supplying a cognitive explanation.

Evidence in the complete study note

Artificial intelligence studies systems that perform tasks requiring intelligence: reasoning, learning, planning, perception and language. Applied AI builds useful solutions; cognitive AI uses computational models to investigate biological intelligence. A model should be compared with human behavior or experimental observations before claiming it explains human thought.AI01
Thinking humanly models human mental processes; thinking rationally derives conclusions by valid logic. Acting humanly seeks humanlike behavior; acting rationally selects actions expected to achieve objectives. Thought processes and observed behavior are different evaluation targets.AI02
The conversational Turing test asks whether a judge can reliably distinguish a machine from a human through their dialogue. It requires language use, knowledge, reasoning and often learning. It tests an operational behavior criterion, not proof of consciousness. Cognitive models can be tested against response times, errors and psychological experiments.AI02

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Brain measurements can provide evidence, but measurement alone does not construct the computational thought model requested.

B · correct — Replicating aspects of thought in a computational model provides a theory whose behavior can be tested.

C · incorrect — Psychological experiments can test a model, but experiments alone do not supply the computational representation asked for.

D · incorrect — More capable hardware supplies resources without itself representing a theory of human thought.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

Correct answer: B — They reduce the search space and speed up the search process.

Problem knowledge guides search toward promising states, often reducing explored nodes and time. It does not universally guarantee optimality or replace a search algorithm. Evidence: PDF 24.

Evidence in the complete study note

A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost or evaluates promise using problem-specific knowledge. It can reduce explored work, but computing it also costs time. Uninformed algorithms use only the problem definition and known costs; UCS remains uninformed despite using g.AI17
Admissibility suffices for optimal A* tree search; graph search that never reopens CLOSED states normally requires consistency. With an admissible inconsistent heuristic, reopen states when g improves. Test a goal when removed at minimum f. Completeness also needs finite branching and positive lower-bounded costs in infinite spaces. Worst-case time and memory can be exponential; no heuristic universally guarantees speed.AI18

Question 163

Which general characterization says that search uses problem-specific knowledge to estimate remaining cost, without itself requiring either non-overestimation or an edge-by-edge consistency inequality?

  • A. Admissible heuristic
  • B. Consistent heuristic
  • C. Informed heuristic
  • D. Dominance comparison between heuristics

Adapted from

  • Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 646

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

AI-S05 · Related search and game-evaluation methods

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

AI-S05 · Related search and game-evaluation methods

Correct answer: C — Informed heuristic

Informed search adds problem-specific knowledge to guide exploration, often through a remaining-cost estimate. That general characterization does not guarantee admissibility or consistency, which impose additional mathematical conditions. Dominance instead compares two estimates pointwise. The question asks for the broad knowledge-use property rather than one of those stronger conditions or comparisons.

Evidence in the complete study note

A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost or evaluates promise using problem-specific knowledge. It can reduce explored work, but computing it also costs time. Uninformed algorithms use only the problem definition and known costs; UCS remains uninformed despite using g.AI17
A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.AI18
For two admissible heuristics, h₂ dominates h₁ when h₂(n)≥h₁(n) for every node. Dominance compares estimates; it is not itself a condition ensuring that an arbitrary heuristic never overestimates. Both estimates must separately satisfy the relevant admissibility assumptions.AI-S05

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Admissibility adds a non-overestimation bound, stronger than the general knowledge-use characterization requested.

B · incorrect — Consistency adds an edge-by-edge inequality, stronger than the general property requested.

C · correct — Informed heuristic guidance uses problem-specific knowledge to estimate remaining cost or promise.

D · incorrect — Dominance compares the numerical estimates of two heuristics rather than naming general use of problem knowledge.

Correct answer: A — Admissible heuristic

The displayed non-overestimation inequality defines admissibility. Consistency is a different edge condition; with the usual nonnegative heuristic estimates and a zero goal estimate, it implies admissibility for states with a goal path. Thus a consistent heuristic can also satisfy the bound, but consistency is not the name of the property being defined. Informedness and dominance do not independently establish the bound.

Evidence in the complete study note

A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.AI18
For two admissible heuristics, h₂ dominates h₁ when h₂(n)≥h₁(n) for every node. Dominance compares estimates; it is not itself a condition ensuring that an arbitrary heuristic never overestimates. Both estimates must separately satisfy the relevant admissibility assumptions.AI-S05

Choice by choice

A · correct — Admissibility is exactly the non-overestimation property stated by this inequality.

B · incorrect — Consistency is an edge-by-edge inequality with goal normalization, rather than the name of the displayed non-overestimation bound.

C · incorrect — Being informed only means using problem knowledge and does not impose this bound.

D · incorrect — Dominance compares two heuristic estimates and does not by itself bound either one by the true remaining cost.

Question 165

Which forward best-first algorithm ranks frontier nodes by accumulated path cost plus a heuristic estimate of remaining cost?

  • A. Depth-first search
  • B. Breadth-first search
  • C. A* search algorithm
  • D. Hill climbing algorithm

Adapted from

  • Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 648

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI14 · Depth-first search

AI20 · Local optimization and evolutionary search

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI14 · Depth-first search

AI20 · Local optimization and evolutionary search

Correct answer: C — A* search algorithm

A* orders frontier nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n), combining the cost already paid with an estimate of the cost still needed. Estimating future cost is not a backward search frontier. DFS and BFS use depth-related removal orders, while hill climbing improves neighboring complete candidates. Replacing the mistaken backward-search phrase preserves the intended heuristic-and-cost algorithm identification.

Evidence in the complete study note

A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.AI18
BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.AI13
DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.AI14
Local search keeps a complete candidate configuration and improves its objective; the path may be irrelevant. Hill climbing chooses better neighbors. First-improvement accepts the first improvement; steepest-ascent examines all neighbors; stochastic variants choose among improvements. Local maxima, plateaus and ridges can stop progress. Random restarts or limited sideways steps can help without guaranteeing success.AI20

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — DFS follows a stack order and does not inherently combine a heuristic with backward search.

B · incorrect — BFS uses breadth order without requiring heuristics or a backward frontier.

C · correct — A* is forward best-first search using f = g + h.

D · incorrect — Hill climbing selects improving neighbors rather than ordering a frontier by accumulated plus remaining path cost.

Evidence in the complete study note

At a depth cutoff use an evaluation function estimating position desirability. Positive favors the designated MAX player, negative MIN; the scale is a convention, with +1/0/−1 often win/draw/loss. Heuristics improve limited computation, not guarantee victory.AI23
Adversarial search models agents with competing objectives. A game specifies states, player to move, legal actions, successor function, terminal test and utility. Perfect information means previous moves and current state are visible; it does not reveal future choices or imply absence of chance. Zero-sum utility makes one player’s gain the other’s loss.AI22

Question 167

Which component is the scoring mapping that assigns a heuristic desirability value to a game state, rather than a search, pruning or sampling procedure?

  • A. Minimax algorithm
  • B. Alpha-beta pruning
  • C. Monte Carlo simulation
  • D. Evaluation function

Adapted from

  • Computer Science MCQ practice collection · Question 650

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Read the definition and the classification axis requested; distinguish the defining purpose from supporting techniques or implementation resources.

Study-guide sections

AI23 · Alpha–beta and game evaluation

AI22 · Games and minimax

AI-S05 · Related search and game-evaluation methods

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI23 · Alpha–beta and game evaluation

AI22 · Games and minimax

AI-S05 · Related search and game-evaluation methods

Correct answer: D — Evaluation function

An evaluation function assigns a desirability score to a game state, especially when search stops at a depth cutoff. Minimax uses scores to choose moves, and alpha–beta avoids branches that cannot alter the backed-up result. Monte Carlo sampling can estimate values from possible continuations, but the sampling procedure is distinct from the mapping whose output is a state score.

Evidence in the complete study note

At a depth cutoff use an evaluation function estimating position desirability. Positive favors the designated MAX player, negative MIN; the scale is a convention, with +1/0/−1 often win/draw/loss. Material counts weighted pieces; mobility counts legal options; territory scores controlled regions. These are different features, often combined. Heuristics improve limited computation, not guarantee victory.AI23
Alpha is MAX’s best lower bound; beta is MIN’s best upper bound. Pass bounds down, update alpha at MAX and beta at MIN, and prune when alpha≥beta. Pruning preserves the minimax value for the same searched tree. Good move ordering increases pruning: worst-case O(b^m), ideal ordering about O(b^(m/2)).AI23
Adversarial search models agents with competing objectives. A game specifies states, player to move, legal actions, successor function, terminal test and utility. Perfect information means previous moves and current state are visible; it does not reveal future choices or imply absence of chance. Zero-sum utility makes one player’s gain the other’s loss.AI22
A Monte Carlo game simulation samples possible continuations and uses their outcomes to estimate position value. An evaluation function is the scoring mapping itself; sampling is one way of obtaining an estimate, while minimax backs values up and alpha–beta removes branches that cannot affect that backed-up decision.AI-S05

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Minimax backs values up through competing choices; it uses state scores rather than being the score mapping itself.

B · incorrect — Alpha–beta pruning skips branches that cannot affect a minimax decision; it is not the scoring mapping.

C · incorrect — Monte Carlo simulation samples continuations whose outcomes may estimate value; sampling is a procedure, not the score mapping itself.

D · correct — An evaluation function maps a state to its estimated desirability score.

Question 177

Which reasoning type guarantees that if premises are true, the conclusion is also true?

  • A. Inductive Reasoning
  • B. Abductive Reasoning
  • C. Deductive Reasoning
  • D. Probabilistic Reasoning

Source

  • Artificial Intelligence review questions · Question 3

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations.

Study-guide sections

AI28 · Deduction, induction and abduction

AI29 · Probability and uncertain models

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI28 · Deduction, induction and abduction

AI29 · Probability and uncertain models

Correct answer: C — Deductive reasoning.

AI28 defines deduction by truth-preserving rules and contrasts induction’s revisable generalizations and abduction’s plausible explanations. With valid deductive inference and true premises, the conclusion must be true. Probabilistic support expresses uncertainty rather than this logical guarantee, so deductive is the relevant reasoning type.

Evidence in the complete study note

Deduction applies truth-preserving rules: all people are mortal; Ada is a person; therefore Ada is mortal. Induction generalizes observations to a broader rule and can be overturned by new examples. Abduction proposes a plausible explanation: wet ground suggests rain, although sprinklers could explain it. Analogy transfers a pattern between similar situations.AI28
Probability describes uncertainty about events. P(¬A)=1−P(A); P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0. Bayes gives P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E): posterior equals likelihood times prior divided by evidence probability. For mutually exclusive exhaustive hypotheses, P(E)=ΣiP(E|Hi)P(Hi).AI29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Induction generalizes beyond observations and can be overturned by new examples.

B · incorrect — Abduction proposes plausible explanations without guaranteeing that they are true.

C · correct — Valid deductive rules preserve truth from true premises to the conclusion.

D · incorrect — Probability can quantify uncertain conclusions rather than provide the stated deductive guarantee.

AI15 · Uniform-cost search and Dijkstra

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

Correct answer: C — f(n)=g(n)+h(n).

AI18 directly defines A* evaluation as actual start-to-node cost g plus estimated node-to-goal cost h. This estimates a solution cost through the node. Using only h is greedy best-first, using only g is uniform-cost selection, and multiplication is not the A* rule.

Evidence in the complete study note

A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.AI18
UCS uses a priority queue ordered by actual accumulated path cost g(n). Remove a minimum-g node; accept a goal when removed, not when first generated. Relax each edge: if a cheaper path is found, update its frontier cost and parent.AI15
Best-first is a family that orders OPEN by an evaluation function. Greedy best-first uses f=h and removes the smallest estimate, ignoring the cost already paid. It can choose an expensive route, loop without duplicate checks, or follow an infinite misleading branch. On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, but not generally optimal. Its implicit finite-tree worst case can be O(b^m).AI17

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Using h alone is greedy best-first rather than A* evaluation.

B · incorrect — Using g alone is uniform-cost ordering and omits the remaining-cost estimate.

C · correct — A* adds the accumulated path cost and estimated remaining cost.

D · incorrect — The defined evaluation is a sum, not a product.

Question 180

Which reflex architecture maintains an internal world state and applies condition–action rules to that modeled state, rather than using only the current percept?

  • A. Simple Reflex Agent
  • B. Goal-Based Agent
  • C. Model-Based Reflex Agent
  • D. Learning Agent

Study-guide sections

AI06 · Simple and model-based reflex agents

AI07 · Goals, utility and model updates

AI08 · Learning-agent components

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI06 · Simple and model-based reflex agents

AI07 · Goals, utility and model updates

AI08 · Learning-agent components

Correct answer: C — Model-Based Reflex Agent

Model-based reflex agents update internal state from previous state, action and current observation, using models of world change and action effects. They then apply rules to that modeled state. Simple reflex agents lack persistent world-state memory. Goal-based and learning capabilities may coexist with a model, but the question specifically asks for the reflex architecture defined by state maintenance and rule application.

Evidence in the complete study note

A simple reflex agent matches condition–action rules against the current percept only: if dirty, clean. It has no persistent world-state memory. This is adequate when the current observation contains everything needed for its rule, but partial observability can make the same percept require different actions.AI06
A model-based reflex agent maintains internal state using the previous state, previous action, current percept, and models of world change and action effects. It then applies rules to that state. Both kinds can use condition–action rules; memory and a world model distinguish them.AI06
A goal-based agent considers future action sequences that reach a desired state. A utility-based agent compares degrees of desirability and trade-offs, choosing maximum expected utility: EU(a)=Σs P(s|a,evidence)U(s). Reaching the destination is a goal; balancing arrival time, safety and cost requires preferences among outcomes.AI07
The performance element selects actions. The learning element changes the agent to improve future performance. The critic evaluates behavior against a performance standard and supplies feedback. The problem generator suggests exploratory actions likely to yield useful experience.AI08

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Simple reflex uses only the current percept without persistent world-state memory.

B · incorrect — Goal-based choice uses future sequences reaching desired states, whereas the requested architecture applies reflex rules to modeled state.

C · correct — Model-based reflex maintains internal state and applies rules to that state.

D · incorrect — Learning concerns improving the agent from experience rather than naming this reflex architecture.

Question 182

Which search algorithm is guaranteed to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?

  • A. Depth-First Search
  • B. Depth-Limited Search
  • C. Breadth-First Search
  • D. Best-First Search

Source

  • Artificial Intelligence review questions · Question 8

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI14 · Depth-first search

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI14 · Depth-first search

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

Correct answer: C — Breadth-first search.

AI13 says BFS explores levels in increasing depth and minimizes the number of edges. An unweighted graph gives equal step costs, making that shortest-path property applicable with visited-state tracking. DFS or a fixed depth limit does not guarantee minimum depth, and generic best-first needs its evaluation rule specified.

Evidence in the complete study note

BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.AI13
DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.AI14
DLS runs DFS to depth ℓ and reports cutoff separately from failure. It misses goals deeper than ℓ. Iterative deepening runs DLS with limits 0,1,2,…; for finite b it finds the shallowest solution with O(b^d) time and O(bd) frontier space, optimal for equal step costs. Repeated shallow work is small compared with the deepest level.AI16

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — DFS can reach a longer path first and is not generally optimal.

B · incorrect — A depth limit can miss a solution or return a nonshortest path within its bound.

C · correct — BFS explores increasing edge counts and finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph.

D · incorrect — Best-first is a family; an unspecified evaluation rule does not guarantee shortest paths.

Question 185

What is the main limitation of Depth-First Search regarding completeness?

Study-guide sections

AI14 · Depth-first search

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI14 · Depth-first search

Correct answer: B — Cycles or infinite branches can prevent finding an existing solution.

AI14 says DFS can fail on infinite paths or cycles and is not generally optimal. Without suitable restrictions or duplicate handling, it may never return to a pending branch containing a goal. Finite visited-state graph traversal changes that result; the limitation is therefore not that DFS only works on trees or always returns a bad path.

Evidence in the complete study note

DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.AI14
Implicit-tree worst-case time is O(b^m), and space is O(bm) when pending siblings are stored, or O(m) for path-only recursive generation. DFS is not generally optimal and can fail on infinite paths or cycles. On a finite graph, visited-state tracking makes traversal complete but needs O(V) storage. Do not confuse the O(b^m) worst-case time bound with the DFS space bounds above.AI14

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — DFS is usually memory-efficient; excess storage is not its defining completeness failure.

B · correct — It may follow an infinite branch or cycle indefinitely while a solution waits elsewhere.

C · incorrect — A returned path can be optimal by coincidence; always suboptimal is too strong.

D · incorrect — DFS also traverses graphs, especially with visited-state tracking.

Correct answers (select all): B, C, D — Reinforcement Learning; Unsupervised Learning; Deep Learning

Unsupervised learning discovers structure without target labels. Reinforcement learning can learn from rewards rather than correct-action target examples. Deep learning is an architecture family and can be trained with unsupervised or reinforcement objectives, so it also need not require labeled input-target data. Supervised learning is specifically defined by those labeled pairs. The capability wording permits both regimes and architecture families to be judged accurately.

Evidence in the complete study note

Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples. Classification predicts discrete labels, such as institution generations or spam/nonspam; regression predicts numeric quantities, such as prices. Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast outcomes and can use either. Specify the target before choosing a method.AI31
Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features. Good clusters have high within-cluster similarity and low between-cluster similarity under an appropriate distance. K-means alternates assignment to nearest centroids and centroid updates.AI32
An RL agent observes state information, takes an action, receives reward and a new observation, and improves its policy to maximize expected cumulative reward. Rewards evaluate outcomes rather than supply the correct action label. Rewards may be delayed; not every correct-looking action receives immediate reward.AI33
ANNs, genetic search and reinforcement learning all improve candidate behavior or performance through experience in different ways. Deep learning is an architecture family usable with supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement objectives. Decision trees and deep models may both be supervised. To distinguish learning regimes, specify labels, reward or unlabeled structure.AI43

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Supervised learning uses labeled examples by definition.

B · correct — RL learns through rewards and interaction, without requiring labeled correct actions.

C · correct — Unsupervised learning explicitly seeks structure without target labels.

D · correct — Deep learning can use unlabeled or reward objectives, so labels are not inherently required.

Question 187

For A* tree search with finite branching, step costs bounded below by a positive constant, goal testing on removal and h(goal)=0, which listed heuristic condition is the weakest sufficient guarantee of optimality? Treat monotone as synonymous with consistent.

  • A. Consistent
  • B. Admissible (never overestimates the actual cost)
  • C. Monotone
  • D. Domain-independent

Adapted from

  • Artificial Intelligence review questions · Question 13

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

Correct answer: B — Admissible (never overestimates the actual cost)

Admissibility requires that a heuristic never overestimate the true cheapest remaining cost. It suffices for optimal A* tree search under the stated cost and goal-testing assumptions. Consistency, also called monotonicity here, is stronger and is particularly important when graph search permanently closes states. Domain independence is unrelated to the optimality condition. Asking for the weakest sufficient listed condition distinguishes admissibility from the stronger alternatives.

Evidence in the complete study note

A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.AI18
Admissibility suffices for optimal A* tree search; graph search that never reopens CLOSED states normally requires consistency. With an admissible inconsistent heuristic, reopen states when g improves. Test a goal when removed at minimum f. Completeness also needs finite branching and positive lower-bounded costs in infinite spaces. Worst-case time and memory can be exponential; no heuristic universally guarantees speed.AI18

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Consistency is sufficient but stronger than the weakest listed condition for tree A*.

B · correct — Admissibility is sufficient for optimal tree A* under the stated assumptions.

C · incorrect — Monotonicity is consistency here and is stronger than necessary for the tree-search guarantee.

D · incorrect — Domain independence is not a heuristic optimality condition.

Correct answer: C — Semantic networks.

AI24 defines semantic networks using concept nodes and labeled relations such as is-a. That matches the node/arc representation in the stem. A semantic network connects concept nodes by labeled relations such as is-a. Frames describe stereotyped entities through slots, values and defaults. A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with conditional probability tables; its joint distribution factors as the product of each node’s probability given its parents. Question 193

  • B. Making educated guesses from patterns
  • C. Finding the best explanation for a set of observations
  • D. Using probability to decide outcomes

Study-guide sections

AI28 · Deduction, induction and abduction

AI29 · Probability and uncertain models

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI28 · Deduction, induction and abduction

AI29 · Probability and uncertain models

Correct answer: C — Finding a plausible best explanation for observations.

AI28 illustrates abduction with wet ground suggesting rain while allowing sprinklers as another cause. It proposes an explanatory hypothesis rather than guaranteeing truth or merely generalizing a pattern. C gives that explanatory role. Probability may rank hypotheses, but numerical probability alone is not the definition of abductive reasoning.

Evidence in the complete study note

Deduction applies truth-preserving rules: all people are mortal; Ada is a person; therefore Ada is mortal. Induction generalizes observations to a broader rule and can be overturned by new examples. Abduction proposes a plausible explanation: wet ground suggests rain, although sprinklers could explain it. Analogy transfers a pattern between similar situations.AI28
Probability describes uncertainty about events. P(¬A)=1−P(A); P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0. Bayes gives P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E): posterior equals likelihood times prior divided by evidence probability. For mutually exclusive exhaustive hypotheses, P(E)=ΣiP(E|Hi)P(Hi).AI29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Certain truth-preserving conclusions describe valid deduction rather than explanatory abduction.

B · incorrect — Pattern-based generalization is closer to induction and omits the explanatory-hypothesis requirement.

C · correct — Abduction seeks a plausible explanation for observed evidence without guaranteeing that explanation.

AI09 · Environment dimensions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI09 · Environment dimensions

Correct answer: B — Deterministic, Static, Discrete

Chess has discrete positions and legal moves. Given the selected move, the resulting position is determined by the rules rather than random outcome sampling. In untimed play, the environment does not change while the player deliberates, so the relevant classification is static. Opponent choice is strategic uncertainty rather than dice-like stochasticity. Specifying untimed play excludes the semidynamic effect of a score-affecting clock.

Evidence in the complete study note

Fully observable means sensors reveal relevant state; partially observable means relevant information is hidden or noisy. Deterministic means state and action determine the next state; stochastic means outcomes involve randomness. Strategic uncertainty about an opponent is distinct from dice-like randomness.AI09
Episodic decisions are independent; sequential decisions affect later situations. Static worlds do not change while deliberating; dynamic ones do. A clock affecting score makes an otherwise static game semidynamic. Discrete quantities have distinct alternatives; continuous quantities vary along real-valued ranges. Known versus unknown concerns knowledge of the transition model, not observability.AI09

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Chess moves are discrete, and opponent strategy is not dice-like stochasticity.

B · correct — Untimed chess is deterministic given chosen moves, static while deliberating and discrete.

C · incorrect — Ordinary chess transition outcomes are deterministic given chosen moves rather than stochastic.

D · incorrect — Chess is discrete rather than continuous, and a clock gives semidynamic rather than this classification.

Study-guide references

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI15 · Uniform-cost search and Dijkstra

Correct answer: C — Uninformed search.

AI17 says uninformed methods use the problem definition and known costs without a problem-specific remaining-cost estimate. This is the usual blind-search meaning. Informed or heuristic search explicitly adds such estimates, and best-first is a broad ordering family that may use heuristic information rather than naming the blind category.

Evidence in the complete study note

A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost or evaluates promise using problem-specific knowledge. It can reduce explored work, but computing it also costs time. Uninformed algorithms use only the problem definition and known costs; UCS remains uninformed despite using g.AI17
UCS uses a priority queue ordered by actual accumulated path cost g(n). Remove a minimum-g node; accept a goal when removed, not when first generated. Relax each edge: if a cheaper path is found, update its frontier cost and parent.AI15

A · incorrect — Informed search adds problem-specific guidance beyond the basic problem definition.

B · incorrect — Heuristic search uses the extra estimate excluded by the stem.

D · incorrect — Best-first specifies evaluation-based ordering and is not generally synonymous with blind search.

Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples. Question 198

For greedy best-first search on an implicit finite tree with branching factor b and maximum depth m, what is the standard worst-case node-count time bound?

  • A. O(m)
  • B. O(b*m)
  • C. O(b^m)
  • D. O(log m)

Adapted from

  • Artificial Intelligence review questions · Question 24

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

Correct answer: C — O(b^m)

Greedy best-first ordering can be misled by a heuristic and may need to explore an exponentially large portion of the finite search tree. With branching factor b and depth m, the standard worst-case generated-node bound is O(b^m). This is a node-count convention rather than a claim about every priority-queue implementation or all best-first algorithms. The explicit algorithm and tree model determine the bound.

Evidence in the complete study note

Best-first is a family that orders OPEN by an evaluation function. Greedy best-first uses f=h and removes the smallest estimate, ignoring the cost already paid. It can choose an expensive route, loop without duplicate checks, or follow an infinite misleading branch. On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, but not generally optimal. Its implicit finite-tree worst case can be O(b^m).AI17

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A misleading heuristic can force exponentially many nodes, so a bound merely linear in maximum depth m is insufficient.

B · incorrect — O(bm) is a familiar DFS storage form, not this generic search-time guarantee.

C · correct — The specified implicit finite-tree worst case can require O(b^m) nodes.

D · incorrect — A logarithmic-in-depth bound is insufficient when the search can explore an exponential number of tree nodes.

Question 201

Which listed term is a reasoning method rather than one of the common learning regimes classified by availability of target labels?

  • A. Supervised Learning
  • B. Unsupervised Learning
  • C. Deductive reasoning
  • D. Semi-supervised Learning

Adapted from

  • Artificial Intelligence review questions · Question 27

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Translate the statement carefully, then check the scope of its quantifiers, connectives or inference rule. Distinguish guaranteed consequences from plausible generalizations or explanations.

Study-guide sections

AI31 · Supervised learning and prediction

AI32 · Unsupervised, semi-supervised and active learning

AI28 · Deduction, induction and abduction

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI31 · Supervised learning and prediction

AI32 · Unsupervised, semi-supervised and active learning

AI28 · Deduction, induction and abduction

Correct answer: C — Deductive reasoning

Supervised, unsupervised and semi-supervised learning differ in the target labels available during training. Deductive reasoning instead derives consequences from premises using truth-preserving rules. Deduction can be used inside a learning system, so the distinction is not that the two can never coexist. The question separates a reasoning method from the conventional label-availability taxonomy.

Evidence in the complete study note

Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled input–target examples. Classification predicts discrete labels, such as institution generations or spam/nonspam; regression predicts numeric quantities, such as prices. Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to forecast outcomes and can use either. Specify the target before choosing a method.AI31
Unsupervised learning seeks structure without target labels: clustering groups similar examples; association finds co-occurrence; dimensionality reduction compresses features. Good clusters have high within-cluster similarity and low between-cluster similarity under an appropriate distance. K-means alternates assignment to nearest centroids and centroid updates.AI32
Semi-supervised learning combines some labels with additional unlabeled data. Active learning chooses informative cases for an oracle to label; it still uses labels. “Exploratory learning” is not an exclusive standard synonym: it can mean unsupervised exploration or active data acquisition, so define the feedback. A task named summarization or time-series analysis is not automatically supervised; its training targets determine that.AI32
Deduction applies truth-preserving rules: all people are mortal; Ada is a person; therefore Ada is mortal. Induction generalizes observations to a broader rule and can be overturned by new examples. Abduction proposes a plausible explanation: wet ground suggests rain, although sprinklers could explain it. Analogy transfers a pattern between similar situations.AI28

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Supervised learning uses labeled input–target pairs, so it is a label-availability learning regime.

B · incorrect — Unsupervised learning has no supplied targets and discovers structure, so it is a label-availability regime.

C · correct — Deduction derives truth-preserving consequences from premises rather than naming a label-availability regime.

D · incorrect — Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled data, so it is a label-availability regime.

Question 202

In adversarial search, what makes it different from traditional search?

  • A. It only uses one agent
  • B. Multiple agents with conflicting goals compete in the same search space
  • C. It guarantees the optimal solution always
  • D. It does not use evaluation functions

Source

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Study-guide sections

AI22 · Games and minimax

AI23 · Alpha–beta and game evaluation

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI22 · Games and minimax

AI23 · Alpha–beta and game evaluation

Correct answer: B — Competing agents with conflicting objectives.

AI22 defines adversarial search by agents with competing objectives and gives minimax for opposition. That distinguishes it from a single-agent path search. It can use evaluation functions at cutoffs, and its best-outcome guarantee is conditional on the modeled game and opponent, not an unconditional guarantee that every implementation finds a globally optimal solution.

Evidence in the complete study note

Adversarial search models agents with competing objectives. A game specifies states, player to move, legal actions, successor function, terminal test and utility. Perfect information means previous moves and current state are visible; it does not reveal future choices or imply absence of chance. Zero-sum utility makes one player’s gain the other’s loss.AI22
At a depth cutoff use an evaluation function estimating position desirability. Positive favors the designated MAX player, negative MIN; the scale is a convention, with +1/0/−1 often win/draw/loss. Material counts weighted pieces; mobility counts legal options; territory scores controlled regions. These are different features, often combined. Heuristics improve limited computation, not guarantee victory.AI23

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A single decision-making agent does not capture the competing-objective feature of adversarial search.

B · correct — Competing agents and conflicting objectives are its defining distinction.

C · incorrect — Guarantees depend on the algorithm, model and search depth, not merely the adversarial label.

D · incorrect — Depth-limited adversarial search commonly uses heuristic evaluation functions.

Question 203

A Depth-Limited Search (DLS) is NOT complete in itself because:

  • A. It uses too much memory
  • B. Solutions beyond the preset depth limit will be missed
  • C. It explores nodes in random order
  • D. It requires a heuristic function

Source

  • Artificial Intelligence review questions · Question 29

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

AI14 · Depth-first search

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

AI14 · Depth-first search

Correct answer: B — A solution beyond the fixed depth limit is missed.

AI16 defines DLS as DFS stopped at depth ℓ and explicitly says it misses goals deeper than that. A fixed limit therefore does not establish completeness for arbitrary problem depths. This is independent of randomized ordering, heuristics or memory use; increasing limits through iterative deepening addresses the depth restriction under its stated assumptions.

Evidence in the complete study note

DLS runs DFS to depth ℓ and reports cutoff separately from failure. It misses goals deeper than ℓ. Iterative deepening runs DLS with limits 0,1,2,…; for finite b it finds the shallowest solution with O(b^d) time and O(bd) frontier space, optimal for equal step costs. Repeated shallow work is small compared with the deepest level.AI16
DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.AI14

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Depth-limited DFS is memory-efficient; excessive memory is not the reason goals are missed.

B · correct — A preset cutoff prevents exploring a solution whose depth exceeds that limit.

C · incorrect — DLS need not use random order; the depth cutoff alone causes the limitation.

D · incorrect — No heuristic is required for depth-limited DFS.

Question 205

What is an 'expanded node' in a search algorithm?

  • A. A node that has been visited but not explored further
  • B. A node selected for further exploration whose neighboring nodes have been generated
  • C. A node removed from the open list
  • D. A node that has reached the goal state

Source

  • Artificial Intelligence review questions · Question 31

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI12 · Frontiers and evaluation criteria

AI13 · Breadth-first search

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI12 · Frontiers and evaluation criteria

AI13 · Breadth-first search

Correct answer: B — A node whose successors have been generated.

AI12 defines expansion as generating successors. B states that action, unlike mere visitation, removal from OPEN or reaching a goal. A node can be removed and goal-tested without expanding it, and discovered frontier nodes await expansion. The criterion is what was generated, not whether the node was seen or selected.

Evidence in the complete study note

A search node records a state plus parent, action, depth and path cost. Expanding a node generates its successors. OPEN or frontier stores discovered candidates awaiting expansion; CLOSED records expanded states. Reaching the same state through different paths does not imply the same node or cost.AI12
BFS removes the oldest frontier entry using a FIFO queue. Start with the root, remove the head, test it, append unseen successors at the tail, and repeat. It explores depths 0,1,2,… and is complete for finite b and a finite-depth goal. It minimizes number of edges, so minimum cost requires equal positive step costs.AI13

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Visiting without generating successors does not meet the definition of expansion.

B · correct — Generating the selected node’s neighboring successor nodes is expansion.

C · incorrect — Removal alone may precede a goal test without generating any successors.

D · incorrect — Goal status is not the definition of expansion; a goal may be accepted without expanding it.

An agent perceives an environment through sensors and acts through actuators or effectors. Cameras sense; motors move. Software sensors may be incoming messages and software actions may be API requests. Humans are agents but are not artificial agents.AI03
A model-based reflex agent maintains internal state using the previous state, previous action, current percept, and models of world change and action effects. It then applies rules to that state. Both kinds can use condition–action rules; memory and a world model distinguish them.AI06

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI07 · Goals, utility and model updates

AI06 · Simple and model-based reflex agents

AI08 · Learning-agent components

Correct answer: B — Choose actions with maximum expected utility, balancing outcome trade-offs.

AI07 defines utility-based agents by comparing desirability and trade-offs and maximizing expected utility over uncertain outcomes. This is broader than merely satisfying a fixed goal. Current-percept rule matching describes simple reflex behavior, and experience-based improvement describes learning, which may coexist with utility choice but does not define it.

Evidence in the complete study note

A goal-based agent considers future action sequences that reach a desired state. A utility-based agent compares degrees of desirability and trade-offs, choosing maximum expected utility: EU(a)=Σs P(s|a,evidence)U(s). Reaching the destination is a goal; balancing arrival time, safety and cost requires preferences among outcomes.AI07
A simple reflex agent matches condition–action rules against the current percept only: if dirty, clean. It has no persistent world-state memory. This is adequate when the current observation contains everything needed for its rule, but partial observability can make the same percept require different actions.AI06
The performance element selects actions. The learning element changes the agent to improve future performance. The critic evaluates behavior against a performance standard and supplies feedback. The problem generator suggests exploratory actions likely to yield useful experience.AI08

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Current-percept condition-action matching describes a simple reflex architecture.

B · correct — Expected-utility maximization explicitly compares trade-offs among uncertain outcomes.

C · incorrect — Goal-reaching planning alone does not rank degrees of desirability among outcomes.

D · incorrect — Learning describes adaptation from feedback, not the utility-based decision criterion itself.

AI23 · Alpha–beta and game evaluation

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI23 · Alpha–beta and game evaluation

Correct answer: D — 0

The convention assigns equal and opposite utilities to the two decisive outcomes. A draw gives neither side an advantage, so its neutral utility is zero under that symmetric scale. Positive one favors MAX and negative one favors MIN; positive infinity would strongly favor MAX rather than indicate neutrality. This is an explicit utility convention, not an intrinsic numerical property of the game outcome.

Evidence in the complete study note

At a depth cutoff use an evaluation function estimating position desirability. Positive favors the designated MAX player, negative MIN; the scale is a convention, with +1/0/−1 often win/draw/loss. Material counts weighted pieces; mobility counts legal options; territory scores controlled regions. These are different features, often combined. Heuristics improve limited computation, not guarantee victory.AI23

Choice by choice

B · incorrect — Under the common stated scale, −1 is a loss rather than a draw.

C · incorrect — Positive infinity is not the draw value in the note’s common scale.

D · correct — Zero is the neutral utility between +1 and −1 under this convention.

The heuristic function h(n) in A* represents:

  • C. The estimated cost from node n to the goal state
  • D. The branching factor at node n

Study-guide sections

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

AI12 · Frontiers and evaluation criteria

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI18 · Admissibility, consistency and A*

AI12 · Frontiers and evaluation criteria

Correct answer: C — Estimated remaining cost from n to a goal.

AI17 defines h as an estimate of remaining cost or promise, and AI18 adds it to accumulated g in A*. Thus C is the heuristic component. Exact start-to-node cost belongs to g, and branching factor b is a search-size parameter rather than a cost-to-go estimate.

Evidence in the complete study note

A heuristic h(n) estimates remaining cost or evaluates promise using problem-specific knowledge. It can reduce explored work, but computing it also costs time. Uninformed algorithms use only the problem definition and known costs; UCS remains uninformed despite using g.AI17
A* orders by f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Admissibility means 0≤h(n)≤h*(n), the true cheapest remaining cost. Consistency means h(n)≤c(n,n′)+h(n′) on every edge, with h(goal)=0; it implies admissibility on states with goal paths. Consistency makes f nondecreasing along a path.AI18
Completeness means finding a solution if one exists under stated assumptions; optimality means returning the best solution. Time counts work, often generated nodes; space counts simultaneous storage. Let b be branching factor, d shallowest goal depth, m maximum search depth, and ℓ a depth limit. Graph-search bounds in vertices V and edges E differ from implicit-tree bounds.AI12

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Exact cost from the start belongs to g(n), not the heuristic h(n).

B · incorrect — Already-traveled path cost is g(n), not estimated future cost.

C · correct — h estimates the remaining cost from the current node to a goal.

D · incorrect — Branching factor counts successor alternatives and is not the heuristic cost estimate.

Question 215

When a doctor proposes a disease as a plausible cause explaining observed symptoms, which term names this explanatory direction of reasoning, rather than a method for numerically ranking hypotheses?

  • A. Deductive Reasoning
  • B. Inductive Reasoning
  • C. Abductive Reasoning
  • D. Probabilistic Reasoning

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Study-guide sections

AI28 · Deduction, induction and abduction

AI29 · Probability and uncertain models

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI28 · Deduction, induction and abduction

AI29 · Probability and uncertain models

Correct answer: C — Abductive Reasoning

Abduction proposes an explanation for observed evidence, such as a disease that could account for symptoms. Other causes may also fit, so the conclusion is not logically guaranteed. Probability can help rank the possible explanations, but that numerical method is distinct from the explanatory direction. Deduction preserves truth from premises, and induction generalizes patterns across cases.

Evidence in the complete study note

Deduction applies truth-preserving rules: all people are mortal; Ada is a person; therefore Ada is mortal. Induction generalizes observations to a broader rule and can be overturned by new examples. Abduction proposes a plausible explanation: wet ground suggests rain, although sprinklers could explain it. Analogy transfers a pattern between similar situations.AI28
Probability describes uncertainty about events. P(¬A)=1−P(A); P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), for P(B)>0. Bayes gives P(H|E)=P(E|H)P(H)/P(E): posterior equals likelihood times prior divided by evidence probability. For mutually exclusive exhaustive hypotheses, P(E)=ΣiP(E|Hi)P(Hi).AI29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Deduction follows truth-preserving implications from premises, not a merely plausible cause inferred from its effects.

B · incorrect — Induction generalizes across observations rather than specifically proposing a cause that explains an observation.

C · correct — Abduction proposes a plausible explanation for observed evidence.

D · incorrect — Probability can rank disease hypotheses, but does not itself name the observation-to-explanation direction.

Correct answer: B — Biased decisions causing unfair outcomes.

AI40 says bias in data or evaluation can create unfair outcomes and calls for checking errors across groups, robustness and oversight. B states the ethical concern directly. Data scarcity may be a technical issue, but little data is not the stated general ethical principle; perfect rationality and inability to process unstructured inputs are false generalizations.

Evidence in the complete study note

Rules offer inspectable domain reasoning but can be brittle and costly to maintain. Learned models handle data-rich patterns but depend on representative data and validation. Search suits explicit action alternatives; probabilistic models suit uncertain evidence. Bias in data or evaluation can create unfair outcomes. Evaluate errors across relevant groups, robustness, privacy and human oversight rather than assuming automation is always beneficial.AI40
Feedforward networks pass signals toward outputs without recurrent state loops; recurrent networks carry state across sequence steps. Training adjusts weights, often through gradients and backpropagation. Backpropagation is not the same as a recurrent connection. ANN is a brain-inspired abstraction, not a literal brain simulation; DL⊂ML⊂AI.AI34
A performance measure defines success externally: safety, useful deliveries, elapsed time, or cost. Rationality depends on that measure, prior knowledge, percept history, and available actions. A rational agent selects the action with the best expected performance given its information.AI04

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Using too little data is not the specific fairness concern described here.

B · correct — Biased data or evaluation can produce unfair or discriminatory decisions.

Question 219

For implicit-tree search with branching factor b and shallowest goal depth d, which is a key memory advantage of iterative deepening over BFS when each depth-limited pass stores pending siblings?

  • A. It finds deeper solutions faster
  • B. It requires storing all nodes at each level in memory
  • C. It uses O(bd) frontier space rather than storing an entire BFS level.
  • D. It does not guarantee completeness

Adapted from

  • Artificial Intelligence review questions · Question 45

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Check how the method selects its next candidate, what information it uses, and which cost, depth or heuristic assumptions the question supplies.

Study-guide sections

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI14 · Depth-first search

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI16 · Depth limits, iterative deepening and two directions

AI13 · Breadth-first search

AI14 · Depth-first search

Correct answer: C — It uses O(bd) frontier space rather than storing an entire BFS level.

Iterative deepening repeats depth-limited DFS while increasing the limit. A pass retains a depth-first path and pending siblings, giving O(bd) frontier space rather than BFS’s potentially exponential level frontier. It remains complete for finite branching and a finite-depth solution, although it repeats some shallow work. The option states the correct memory advantage without claiming that every implementation stores only the current path.

Evidence in the complete study note

DLS runs DFS to depth ℓ and reports cutoff separately from failure. It misses goals deeper than ℓ. Iterative deepening runs DLS with limits 0,1,2,…; for finite b it finds the shallowest solution with O(b^d) time and O(bd) frontier space, optimal for equal step costs. Repeated shallow work is small compared with the deepest level.AI16
The tree contains 1+b+…+b^d nodes through depth d, giving O(b^d) under generation-time goal testing. Expanding depth-d nodes before testing can generate depth d+1 and yields O(b^(d+1)); specify the convention. Explicit finite graph traversal with visited-state tracking takes O(V+E) time and O(V) space.AI13
DFS follows the deepest pending branch using a LIFO stack or recursion. FILO means the same order as LIFO. With the same children as BFS, a left-first DFS visits S,A,C before B; push rightmost children first to pop the leftmost first.AI14

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — IDS repeats shallow work and does not universally find deeper solutions faster than BFS.

B · incorrect — Storing all nodes at a level is BFS-style memory behavior, not the IDS advantage.

C · correct — The stated implementation keeps only a depth-first frontier, requiring O(bd) rather than the BFS level frontier.

D · incorrect — IDS is complete under finite branching and a finite-depth solution, so loss of completeness is not its benefit.

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

AI17 · Heuristics and greedy best-first search

AI19 · Work a heuristic-search example

Correct answer: B — It uses only h and can ignore a cheaper route with a larger estimate.

AI17 defines greedy best-first as f=h, ignoring cost already paid. AI19 demonstrates a route of cost 11 selected greedily while another route costs 4. The heuristic ranking can therefore prefer a worse total solution. Greedy is neither exhaustive nor breadth-first and does not order primarily by actual path cost.

Evidence in the complete study note

Best-first is a family that orders OPEN by an evaluation function. Greedy best-first uses f=h and removes the smallest estimate, ignoring the cost already paid. It can choose an expensive route, loop without duplicate checks, or follow an infinite misleading branch. On a finite graph with full duplicate handling it is complete, but not generally optimal. Its implicit finite-tree worst case can be O(b^m).AI17
For S→A cost 2, S→B cost 1, A→G cost 2, B→G cost 10, set h(A)=2, h(B)=1, h(G)=0. After expanding S, greedy chooses B because 1<2 and can then choose G, returning cost 11. A* compares A:f=2+2=4 and B:f=1+1=2; after B, its G entry costs 11. It next expands A and replaces G with cost 4, which is removed and accepted.AI19

B · correct — Ignoring accumulated cost can favor a seemingly close but expensive route over a cheaper solution.

C · incorrect — Using actual g alone describes UCS, whereas greedy uses h.

D · incorrect — Breadth-first depth order is not the greedy minimum-heuristic policy.
